query.original_query: information density entropy rate of language and LLM reasoning uniform information density

sub_queries.semantic_query: information density entropy rate uniform information density in large language model internal representations and reasoning processing of linguistic predictability and surprisal
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate how information density and entropy rate manifest within the internal representations of large language models during language processing. Using causal tracing and activation patching, we analyze the relationship between token-level surprisal and the uniformity of information distribution across residual stream states. Our analysis reveals that model layers exhibit systematic deviations from uniform information density, with higher surprisal tokens correlating with increased entropy in intermediate representations. We find that attention heads in middle layers selectively compress or expand information content, modulating the local entropy rate in response to linguistic predictability. Results show that the model’s internal processing of surprisal is not uniformly distributed but concentrated in specific MLP and attention sublayers, suggesting a hierarchical encoding of predictability. These findings align with predictions from the uniform information density hypothesis, while also revealing layer-specific mechanisms that adjust information rate during autoregressive generation. Our work provides a mechanistic account of how surprisal and entropy constraints shape internal representations in transformer language models.

sub_queries.semantic_query: uniform information density theory entropy rate linguistic predictability and information density in human language processing and comprehension
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated the predictions of the Uniform Information Density (UID) hypothesis by examining the relationship between entropy rate, linguistic predictability, and processing difficulty during naturalistic sentence comprehension. Participants read English sentences while their eye movements were recorded using an eye-tracker. We calculated word-level information density (surprisal) and local entropy from a large language model-based parser, and measured processing effort via gaze duration and regression probability. Results indicate that regions of high surprisal (low predictability) elicited longer first-pass reading times and increased regressive saccades, consistent with increased processing cost. Critically, we observed a significant interaction between local entropy and surprisal: the effect of high surprisal on reading times was attenuated in high-entropy contexts, where multiple lexical alternatives are plausible. This finding supports the hypothesis that comprehenders maintain a preferred rate of information intake, actively modulating processing resources to avoid peaks in information density. The results are discussed in the context of entropy rate constancy and the role of probabilistic expectations in real-time language comprehension.

papers.title: Comparison of Structural Parsers and Neural Language Models as Surprisal Estimators
papers.research_question: How do structural parsers and neural language models compare as surprisal estimators for predicting human sentence processing difficulty?
papers.core_contribution: The proposed structural parser, which incorporates strong linguistic generalizations, achieves comparable or superior fits to human reading times compared to neural language models trained on much more data. Among GPT-2 models, smaller models with fewer parameters fit human data better when training data is held constant.
papers.conclusion: Incremental parsers that embody strong linguistic generalizations are more appropriate as computational-level models of human sentence processing than deep neural language models, which require orders of magnitude more training data and do not provide a better fit to human reading behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Surprisal estimates from the structural parser deliver comparable and often superior fits to self-paced reading and eye-tracking data compared to neural language models.
Among GPT-2 models sharing the same architecture and training data, there is a negative correlation between parameter count and fit to self-paced reading and eye-tracking data.
The character-based morphological word model in the structural parser makes a large contribution to regression model fit, suggesting a role for subword information in sentence processing.
Surprisal estimates from the structural parser and 5-gram model did not contribute as much to fMRI data model fit compared to neural LMs, suggesting different measures are sensitive to different aspects of processing difficulty.
The relationship between language model perplexity and psychometric predictive power is influenced by primary architecture and training data amount, not just model capacity.
future_direction: Future work should continue to focus on incorporating relevant linguistic generalizations into concrete models and evaluating their predictions on human subject data.
papers.abstract: Expectation-based theories of sentence processing posit that processing difficulty is determined by predictability in context. While predictability quantified via surprisal has gained empirical support, this representation-agnostic measure leaves open the question of how to best approximate the human comprehender's latent probability model. This article first describes an incremental left-corner parser that incorporates information about common linguistic abstractions such as syntactic categories, predicate-argument structure, and morphological rules as a computational-level model of sentence processing. The article then evaluates a variety of structural parsers and deep neural language models as cognitive models of sentence processing by comparing the predictive power of their surprisal estimates on self-paced reading, eye-tracking, and fMRI data collected during real-time language processing. The results show that surprisal estimates from the proposed left-corner processing model deliver comparable and often superior fits to self-paced reading and eye-tracking data when compared to those from neural language models trained on much more data. This may suggest that the strong linguistic generalizations made by the proposed processing model may help predict humanlike processing costs that manifest in latency-based measures, even when the amount of training data is limited. Additionally, experiments using Transformer-based language models sharing the same primary architecture and training data show a surprising negative correlation between parameter count and fit to self-paced reading and eye-tracking data. These findings suggest that large-scale neural language models are making weaker generalizations based on patterns of lexical items rather than stronger, more humanlike generalizations based on linguistic structure.

papers.title: Large Language Models Are Human-Like Internally
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether surprisal (negative log probability) from internal layers of large language models aligns with human sentence processing data, and whether the alignment varies by layer depth and the type of human measure (behavioral vs. neurophysiological).
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that surprisal from internal layers of larger language models aligns well with human sentence processing data, challenging prior conclusions that focused on final layers. Additionally, it finds that earlier layers align with fast human measures (e.g., gaze duration) and later layers with slower measures (e.g., N400).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that larger language models are cognitively plausible when internal layers are considered, and that different layers correspond to different stages of human sentence processing, advocating for layer-wise alignment in cognitive modeling.
papers.key_findings:
Surprisal from internal layers of larger LMs aligns with human sentence processing data as well as or better than smaller LMs.
The last layer does not yield the best alignment; the best layer varies by human measure.
Earlier layers align better with fast human measures (e.g., first-pass gaze duration, self-paced reading time), while later layers align better with slower measures (e.g., N400, MAZE processing time).
When considering the best internal layer, larger LMs show a positive scaling effect (larger models have higher ∆LL) for most human measures.
The alignment patterns are consistent across multiple languages (tested on MECO corpus).
papers.limitation: The study is focused on naturalistic reading corpora and does not include controlled experiments on syntactic ambiguity or grammatical violation, which are known challenges for surprisal theory.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other probability-based measures such as entropy and entropy reduction.
Combine the internal layer approach with linguistically-motivated neural models.
papers.abstract: Recent cognitive modeling studies have reported that larger language models (LMs) exhibit a poorer fit to human reading behavior (Oh and Schuler, 2023b; Shain et al., 2024; Kuribayashi et al., 2024), leading to claims of their cognitive implausibility. In this paper, we revisit this argument through the lens of mechanistic interpretability and argue that prior conclusions were skewed by an exclusive focus on the final layers of LMs. Our analysis reveals that next-word probabilities derived from internal layers of larger LMs align with human sentence processing data as well as, or better than, those from smaller LMs. This alignment holds consistently across behavioral (self-paced reading times, gaze durations, MAZE task processing times) and neurophysiological (N400 brain potentials) measures, challenging earlier mixed results and suggesting that the cognitive plausibility of larger LMs has been underestimated. Furthermore, we first identify an intriguing relationship between LM layers and human measures: earlier layers correspond more closely with fast gaze durations, while later layers better align with relatively slower signals such as N400 potentials and MAZE processing times. Our work opens new avenues for interdisciplinary research at the intersection of mechanistic interpretability and cognitive modeling.

papers.title: Joint processing of linguistic properties in brains and language models
papers.research_question: What linguistic properties are responsible for the alignment between brain recordings (fMRI) and language model representations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a direct approach to evaluate joint linguistic processing in brains and language models by removing specific linguistic properties from model representations, showing this significantly decreases brain alignment, with syntactic properties having the largest effect.
papers.conclusion: The direct approach provides clear evidence that specific linguistic information, particularly syntactic properties, underlies the alignment between brain and language models, opening new avenues for mapping joint information processing.
papers.key_findings:
Removing each tested linguistic property (surface, syntactic, semantic) results in a significant decrease in brain alignment across all layers of BERT and GPT-2.
Syntactic properties (Top Constituents and Tree Depth) have the largest effect on the trend of brain alignment across model layers.
Top Constituents affects alignment in all language brain regions, while Tree Depth specifically affects temporal (ATL, PTL) and frontal (IFG, MFG) regions.
Semantic properties (Tense, Subject Number, Object Number) affect alignment more specifically in regions like the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC).
The method reveals that different linguistic properties are important for alignment in different brain regions and sub-regions.
papers.limitation:
The removal approach may also remove information correlated with the removed linguistic property due to dataset limitations.
Substantial brain alignment remains after removing all tested properties, indicating not all relevant linguistic properties have been accounted for.
The study is limited to English language stimuli and two language models (BERT and GPT-2).
future_direction: Incorporate additional linguistic properties to fully characterize joint processing.
Investigate larger language models beyond BERT and GPT-2.
Extend the approach to languages beyond English.
papers.abstract: Language models have been shown to be very effective in predicting brain recordings of subjects experiencing complex language stimuli. For a deeper understanding of this alignment, it is important to understand the correspondence between the detailed processing of linguistic information by the human brain versus language models. We investigate this correspondence via a direct approach, in which we eliminate information related to specific linguistic properties in the language model representations and observe how this intervention affects the alignment with fMRI brain recordings obtained while participants listened to a story. We investigate a range of linguistic properties (surface, syntactic, and semantic) and find that the elimination of each one results in a significant decrease in brain alignment. Specifically, we find that syntactic properties (i.e. Top Constituents and Tree Depth) have the largest effect on the trend of brain alignment across model layers. These findings provide clear evidence for the role of specific linguistic information in the alignment between brain and language models, and open new avenues for mapping the joint information processing in both systems. We make the code publicly available [https://github.com/subbareddy248/linguistic-properties-brain-alignment].

papers.title: Probing Information Distribution in Transformer Architectures through Entropy Analysis
papers.research_question: How does token-level uncertainty, quantified by entropy, evolve across layers and token positions in decoder-only Transformer models, and how does contextual information influence this uncertainty?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an entropy-based framework to analyze information flow in Transformers, revealing how uncertainty evolves non-monotonically across layers and token positions.
papers.conclusion: Entropy analysis provides a powerful, architecture-agnostic tool for interpreting Transformer internal states, complementing traditional metrics and aiding in developing more interpretable models.
papers.key_findings:
Entropy decreases with increasing token position, indicating higher confidence with more context.
Prediction error decreases monotonically with network depth, but entropy shows non-monotonic behavior, increasing in final layers for larger models.
Larger models exhibit broader entropy distributions in intermediate layers and a terminal-layer entropy increase, suggesting increased representational flexibility.
papers.abstract: This work explores entropy analysis as a tool for probing information distribution within Transformer-based architectures. By quantifying token-level uncertainty and examining entropy patterns across different stages of processing, we aim to investigate how information is managed and transformed within these models. As a case study, we apply the methodology to a GPT-based large language model, illustrating its potential to reveal insights into model behavior and internal representations. This approach may offer insights into model behavior and contribute to the development of interpretability and evaluation frameworks for transformer-based models

papers.title: The Information of Large Language Model Geometry
papers.research_question: What information is encoded in the embeddings of large language models, and how does it relate to scaling laws and the auto-regressive structure?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an information-theoretic framework based on conditional entropy to explain scaling laws in LLMs, and analyzes the auto-regressive structure using information gain and regression, showing that information is distributed across tokens.
papers.conclusion: The paper investigates information in LLM embeddings, finding a power law for representation entropy and providing an entropy-based theory for scaling laws. It connects information gain to ridge regression, shows Lasso can pick meaningful tokens, and demonstrates that sentence meaning is distributed across tokens.
papers.key_findings:
Representation entropy follows a power law relationship with model size.
A theory based on conditional entropy explains scaling laws for parameters, flops, and dataset size.
The information gain of new tokens is theoretically connected to ridge regression.
Lasso regression can select meaningful tokens and sometimes outperforms attention weights.
Information is distributed across tokens, not concentrated in specific tokens alone.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the information encoded in the embeddings of large language models (LLMs). We conduct simulations to analyze the representation entropy and discover a power law relationship with model sizes. Building upon this observation, we propose a theory based on (conditional) entropy to elucidate the scaling law phenomenon. Furthermore, we delve into the auto-regressive structure of LLMs and examine the relationship between the last token and previous context tokens using information theory and regression techniques. Specifically, we establish a theoretical connection between the information gain of new tokens and ridge regression. Additionally, we explore the effectiveness of Lasso regression in selecting meaningful tokens, which sometimes outperforms the closely related attention weights. Finally, we conduct controlled experiments, and find that information is distributed across tokens, rather than being concentrated in specific "meaningful" tokens alone.

papers.title: Predictive Coding or Just Feature Discovery? An Alternative Account of Why Language Models Fit Brain Data
papers.research_question: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to embed language representations into a low-dimensional space based on transferability, and shows that this embedding captures the hierarchical organization of language processing in the human brain.
papers.conclusion: The low-dimensional structure of language representations reflects the structure of language representations in the human brain, and the method provides a template for investigating relationships between linguistic and cognitive representations.
papers.key_findings:
The representation embedding matrix reveals a low-dimensional structure where language models and translation models interpolate between word embeddings, syntactic/semantic tasks, and future word embeddings.
The first dimension of this structure corresponds to a hierarchy from low-level to high-level language processing.
This first dimension maps onto the brain's language processing hierarchy, with early auditory areas explained by lower-level features and higher-order areas by later model layers.
The representation embeddings can predict which representations best explain brain activity in different regions.
Most pairs of representations are discriminable based on their brain activity patterns, indicating the embeddings capture brain representation structure.
papers.limitation:
The chosen set of representations may not capture the full diversity of the space.
The use of GloVe as the universal input representation may not be truly universal.
The use of linear networks may underestimate relatedness between tasks.
future_direction: Using an even larger number of representations to better map the space.
Using other universal spaces, such as directly using fMRI data as input.
Exploring regularized nonlinear models for the encoder-decoder networks.
papers.abstract: Many recent studies have shown that representations drawn from neural network language models are extremely effective at predicting brain responses to natural language. But why do these models work so well? One proposed explanation is that language models and brains are similar because they have the same objective: to predict upcoming words before they are perceived. This explanation is attractive because it lends support to the popular theory of predictive coding. We provide several analyses that cast doubt on this claim. First, we show that the ability to predict future words does not uniquely (or even best) explain why some representations are a better match to the brain than others. Second, we show that within a language model, representations that are best at predicting future words are strictly worse brain models than other representations. Finally, we argue in favor of an alternative explanation for the success of language models in neuroscience: These models are effective at predicting brain responses because they generally capture a wide variety of linguistic phenomena.

papers.title: Measuring and Analyzing Intelligence via Contextual Uncertainty in Large Language Models using Information-Theoretic Metrics
papers.research_question: How do large language models process information as context length grows? The paper investigates this by building a quantitative Cognitive Profile for any model using information-theoretic metrics.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a task-agnostic method for building a quantitative Cognitive Profile of LLMs by tracking predictive uncertainty (via the Entropy Decay Curve) and summarizing it with the Information Gain Span, which reveals how models process information and can detect memorization.
papers.conclusion: The Entropy Decay Curve and Information Gain Span offer a principled, task-agnostic way to analyze and compare the internal dynamics of LLMs, revealing differences in how models process information and flagging potential memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models (like Llama 3.3 70.6B) show a sharper decline in uncertainty with context length compared to smaller models.
The Entropy Decay Curve (EDC) is corpus-dependent: easier texts (like Alice's Adventures in Wonderland) lead to lower long-context uncertainty than more complex texts (like Ulysses and Kant's Critique of Judgement).
The EDC can detect memorization (entropy collapse) when long-context uncertainty becomes extremely low, indicating potential data contamination.
The Information Gain Span (IGS) provides a single scalar that summarizes the desirability of the decay pattern (high initial uncertainty and low final uncertainty).
The method provides a quantitative way to compare models and texts without task-specific benchmarks.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a small set of models, corpora, and window lengths, and relies on finite-sample Monte Carlo estimates.
future_direction: Extend coverage to more architectures and training regimes.
Evaluate specialized domains (code, scientific, medical, legal).
Characterize estimator variance and sensitivity to sampling design, and refine contamination tests by combining EDC signals with independent memorization audits.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel on many task-specific benchmarks, yet the mechanisms that drive this success remain poorly understood. We move from asking what these systems can do to asking how they process information. Our contribution is a task-agnostic method that builds a quantitative Cognitive Profile for any model. The profile is built around the Entropy Decay Curve -- a plot of a model's normalised predictive uncertainty as context length grows. Across several state-of-the-art LLMs and diverse texts, the curves expose distinctive, stable profiles that depend on both model scale and text complexity. We also propose the Information Gain Span (IGS) as a single index that summarises the desirability of a decay pattern. Together, these tools offer a principled way to analyse and compare the internal dynamics of modern AI systems.

papers.title: A hierarchy of linguistic predictions during natural language comprehension
papers.research_question: What is the role of prediction in language processing? Specifically, how ubiquitous are predictions and at what levels (syntactic, semantic, phonemic) do they occur?
papers.core_contribution: The brain generates hierarchical predictions during natural language comprehension, with dissociable neural signatures for predictions at the level of syntax, semantics, and phonemes, supporting the ubiquity and multi-level nature of predictive processing.
papers.conclusion: Prediction is a ubiquitous and automatic component of language processing, with the brain spontaneously generating hierarchical predictions across multiple levels of abstraction, from phonemes to meaning.
papers.key_findings:
Brain responses to words are modulated by continuous, probabilistic predictions, and these effects are not confined to constraining contexts or a subset of words.
Predictions are feature-specific, with dissociable neural signatures for syntactic (part-of-speech), semantic, and phonemic prediction errors.
High-level (word) predictions inform low-level (phoneme) predictions, supporting hierarchical predictive processing.
The neural modulation by word surprisal resembles the N400 component and is widespread across the language network.
Syntactic surprisal evokes an early frontal positivity, semantic prediction error a late distributed positivity, and phoneme surprisal an early negativity (similar to N250/PMN).
papers.limitation:
The source of the disentangled predictions from the language model is unknown, as the model uses any available statistical cue, making it unclear which information is used to generate predictions at each level.
There is substantial individual variability in the spatiotemporal signatures of prediction errors, so group-level averages may not be representative of every individual.
future_direction: Test whether the interaction between levels found for phonemes applies to all linguistic levels, or if predictions at some levels (e.g., syntax) are independent.
Understand how predefined, linguistically motivated levels relate to data-driven, model-based levels of prediction.
papers.abstract: Abstract Understanding spoken language requires transforming ambiguous acoustic streams into a hierarchy of representations, from phonemes to meaning. It has been suggested that the brain uses prediction to guide the interpretation of incoming input. However, the role of prediction in language processing remains disputed, with disagreement about both the ubiquity and representational nature of predictions. Here, we address both issues by analysing brain recordings of participants listening to audiobooks, and using a deep neural network (GPT-2) to precisely quantify contextual predictions. First, we establish that brain responses to words are modulated by ubiquitous, probabilistic predictions. Next, we disentangle model-based predictions into distinct dimensions, revealing dissociable signatures of syntactic, phonemic and semantic predictions. Finally, we show that high-level (word) predictions inform low-level (phoneme) predictions, supporting hierarchical predictive processing. Together, these results underscore the ubiquity of prediction in language processing, showing that the brain spontaneously predicts upcoming language at multiple levels of abstraction.

papers.title: Confidence Regulation Neurons in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models represent and regulate uncertainty in next-token predictions? Specifically, what are the roles of entropy neurons and token frequency neurons in confidence calibration?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes two types of confidence-regulation neurons in LLMs: entropy neurons, which modulate output entropy via an unembedding null space and LayerNorm, and token frequency neurons, which adjust the output distribution towards or away from the unigram distribution.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess dedicated neurons for confidence regulation, which operate through specific mechanisms such as writing to the unembedding null space and modulating the distance to the unigram distribution, highlighting the importance of these components for calibration.
papers.key_findings:
Entropy neurons write to an effective null space of the unembedding matrix and use the final LayerNorm scale to modulate output entropy with minimal direct effect on logits.
Token frequency neurons boost or suppress token logits proportionally to their frequency, shifting the output distribution towards or away from the unigram distribution.
These neurons act as hedging mechanisms, increasing loss on correct predictions but preventing loss spikes on incorrect ones.
Entropy neurons are present across various model families and scales (up to 7B parameters).
In induction tasks, entropy neurons increase output entropy to decrease confidence when repeating subsequences.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to decoder-only Transformer-based language models.
Token frequency neurons are identified only in models for which the training corpus is known.
The case study focuses solely on induction.
Entropy neurons might be a byproduct of dropout regularization, as all analyzed models were trained with dropout.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to encoder-decoder models.
Study other potential confidence-regulation mechanisms.
Investigate the role of dropout in the formation of entropy neurons.
Explore interactions between confidence-regulation neurons and other model components.
papers.abstract: Despite their widespread use, the mechanisms by which large language models (LLMs) represent and regulate uncertainty in next-token predictions remain largely unexplored. This study investigates two critical components believed to influence this uncertainty: the recently discovered entropy neurons and a new set of components that we term token frequency neurons. Entropy neurons are characterized by an unusually high weight norm and influence the final layer normalization (LayerNorm) scale to effectively scale down the logits. Our work shows that entropy neurons operate by writing onto an unembedding null space, allowing them to impact the residual stream norm with minimal direct effect on the logits themselves. We observe the presence of entropy neurons across a range of models, up to 7 billion parameters. On the other hand, token frequency neurons, which we discover and describe here for the first time, boost or suppress each token's logit proportionally to its log frequency, thereby shifting the output distribution towards or away from the unigram distribution. Finally, we present a detailed case study where entropy neurons actively manage confidence in the setting of induction, i.e. detecting and continuing repeated subsequences.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: Does Representation Matter? Exploring Intermediate Layers in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What defines a 'good' representation in large language models, and how does the quality of intermediate representations compare to final layers across different architectures and settings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that intermediate layers of LLMs often provide better representations for downstream tasks than final layers, and reveals significant differences in representation quality and evolution between Transformer and State Space Model (SSM) architectures.
papers.conclusion: The research advances understanding of internal representation dynamics in LLMs, highlighting the pivotal role of intermediate layers and the distinct behaviors of Transformer and SSM architectures, providing guidance for model optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers consistently outperform final layers on downstream embedding tasks from the MTEB benchmark.
Prompt entropy in intermediate layers is negatively correlated with MMLU performance for Transformers like Llama3, but not for SSMs like Mamba2.
Transformers exhibit greater representational variability and information compression in intermediate layers, while SSMs show more stable representations across layers.
Training effects on representation quality are most pronounced in intermediate layers, with prompt entropy decreasing and InfoNCE peaking as training progresses.
Extreme input conditions (token repetition, randomness, and length) distinctly affect prompt entropy, particularly in intermediate layers, and a bimodal entropy distribution is observed in Transformer intermediate layers with an unknown cause.
papers.limitation: The cause of the bimodal entropy distribution observed in intermediate layers of Transformer models remains unknown.
future_direction: Investigate the causes of bimodal entropy distributions in intermediate layers.
Explore the development of new metrics specifically tailored to LLMs for representation evaluation.
papers.abstract: Understanding what defines a good representation in large language models (LLMs) is fundamental to both theoretical understanding and practical applications. In this paper, we investigate the quality of intermediate representations in various LLM architectures, including Transformers and State Space Models (SSMs). We find that intermediate layers often yield more informative representations for downstream tasks than the final layers. To measure the representation quality, we adapt and apply a suite of metrics - such as prompt entropy, curvature, and augmentation-invariance - originally proposed in other contexts. Our empirical study reveals significant architectural differences, how representations evolve throughout training, and how factors like input randomness and prompt length affect each layer. Notably, we observe a bimodal pattern in the entropy of some intermediate layers and consider potential explanations tied to training data. Overall, our results illuminate the internal mechanics of LLMs and guide strategies for architectural optimization and training.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: Linear Recency Bias During Training Improves Transformers' Fit to Reading Times
papers.research_question: Does incorporating a recency bias (specifically ALiBi) into Transformer attention improve the fit of surprisal estimates to human reading times, and what is the role of using a mixture of slopes across attention heads?
papers.core_contribution: Incorporating ALiBi (a linear recency bias) during both training and inference improves Transformer surprisal's fit to human reading times, and a mixture of decay slopes across attention heads is crucial for this improvement, enabling the model to track different linguistic dependencies.
papers.conclusion: Incorporating varying rates of memory decay (via ALiBi's mixed slopes) is a promising direction for improving language models and developing cognitive models that better capture human sentence processing behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Surprisal estimates from Transformers with ALiBi show a better fit to human reading times than a standard Transformer baseline.
The improvement is strongest when ALiBi is included during both training and inference, not just at inference time.
Using a uniform slope across all attention heads performs worse than using a mixture of slopes, indicating the mixture is necessary for optimal reading time prediction.
Analysis of attention heads in the ALiBi model shows that heads with higher slopes (stronger recency bias) attend more to shorter-distance argument dependencies, while heads with lower slopes attend more to longer-distance coreference dependencies.
Models with ALiBi during training and inference achieve lower perplexity than the baseline, and a negative relationship exists between perplexity and reading time fit across the tested models.
papers.limitation:
The findings are based on English text and native English speakers, so they may not generalize to other languages.
The regression modeling assumes a linear effect of surprisal on reading times.
papers.abstract: Recent psycholinguistic research has compared human reading times to surprisal estimates from language models to study the factors shaping human sentence processing difficulty. Previous studies have shown a strong fit between surprisal values from Transformers and reading times. However, standard Transformers work with a lossless representation of the entire previous linguistic context, unlike models of human language processing that include memory decay. To bridge this gap, this paper evaluates a modification of the Transformer model that uses ALiBi (Press et al., 2022), a recency bias added to attention scores. Surprisal estimates with ALiBi show an improved fit to human reading times compared to a standard Transformer baseline. A subsequent analysis of attention heads suggests that ALiBi's mixture of slopes -- which determine the rate of memory decay in each attention head -- may play a role in the improvement by helping models with ALiBi to track different kinds of linguistic dependencies.

papers.title: Neural Correlates of Language Models Are Specific to Human Language
papers.research_question: Are correlations between language model hidden states and fMRI brain responses robust to dimensionality concerns, and are they specific to models trained on human language and dependent on positional encoding?
papers.core_contribution: The study confirms that correlations between transformer language model hidden states and human brain activity during language tasks are robust, specific to language-trained models, and heavily dependent on positional encodings.
papers.conclusion: The internal representations of transformer language models are strongly correlated with human brain activity during language processing, and this alignment is specific to language-trained models and relies on positional information.
papers.key_findings:
Removing positional encodings significantly reduces brain-model correlations and distorts the geometric similarity between model and brain representational spaces.
Dimensionality reduction via PCA does not eliminate the correlations, indicating they are not an artifact of the curse of dimensionality.
Models trained on non-linguistic data (protein sequences) show negligible alignment with brain activity, confirming the language-specificity of the effects.
Causal (decoder-only) language models show higher alignment with brain activity than bidirectional models.
The geometric structure of model and brain representations, measured by CKA and Gromov-Wasserstein distance, is similar and degrades when positional information is removed.
papers.limitation:
The dataset includes only 243 stimuli and 6 subjects, limiting statistical power and generalizability.
The head-wise analysis pooled voxels across cortical regions without distinguishing between different regions of interest.
The study uses text-only models and fMRI data from reading tasks; future work should use modality-matched datasets (e.g., audio models with spoken language tasks).
future_direction: Increase the number of subjects and model diversity to improve statistical power and generalizability.
Conduct finer-grained region-of-interest (ROI) by head analysis to reveal differential alignment patterns.
Use modality-matched datasets (e.g., spoken-language tasks with audio models) to disentangle task effects from representational differences.
papers.abstract: Previous work has shown correlations between the hidden states of large language models and fMRI brain responses, on language tasks. These correlations have been taken as evidence of the representational similarity of these models and brain states. This study tests whether these previous results are robust to several possible concerns. Specifically this study shows: (i) that the previous results are still found after dimensionality reduction, and thus are not attributable to the curse of dimensionality; (ii) that previous results are confirmed when using new measures of similarity; (iii) that correlations between brain representations and those from models are specific to models trained on human language; and (iv) that the results are dependent on the presence of positional encoding in the models. These results confirm and strengthen the results of previous research and contribute to the debate on the biological plausibility and interpretability of state-of-the-art large language models.

papers.title: The Generalization Ridge: Information Flow in Natural Language Generation
papers.research_question: In NLG, how does information evolve across layers during training, and how are different layers of the network functionally organized to support generalization versus memorization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces InfoRidge, an information-theoretic framework, and uses it to reveal a 'generalization ridge' in intermediate layers where predictive information peaks, indicating a trade-off between generalization and memorization.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal a consistent generalization ridge in intermediate layers, reflecting a fundamental trade-off between generalization and memorization as information flows deeper into the model.
papers.key_findings:
Predictive information peaks at intermediate layers (the 'generalization ridge') and then declines in final layers.
Incremental information gain is highest in intermediate layers.
Attention patterns show that intermediate layers attend to task-relevant (signal) tokens.
Residual scaling experiments show that under distribution shift, the model relies less on final layers and more on intermediate layers.
The generalization ridge phenomenon persists in multi-token generation scenarios.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models have achieved state-of-the-art performance in natural language generation (NLG), yet their internal mechanisms for synthesizing task-relevant information remain insufficiently understood. While prior studies suggest that intermediate layers often yield more generalizable representations than final layers, how this generalization ability emerges and propagates across layers during training remains unclear. To address this gap, we propose InfoRidge, an information-theoretic framework, to characterize how predictive information-the mutual information between hidden representations and target outputs-varies across depth during training. Our experiments across various models and datasets reveal a consistent non-monotonic trend: predictive information peaks in intermediate layers-forming a generalization ridge-before declining in final layers, reflecting a transition between generalization and memorization. To further investigate this phenomenon, we conduct a set of complementary analyses that leverage residual scaling, attention pattern, and controlled model capacity to characterize layer-wise functional specialization. We further validate our findings with multiple-token generation experiments, verifying that the observed ridge phenomenon persists across decoding steps. Together, these findings offer new insights into the internal mechanisms of transformers and underscore the critical role of intermediate layers in supporting generalization.

papers.title: Inferring the nature of linguistic computations in the brain
papers.research_question: How can we infer the nature of linguistic computations from neural data, and what are the pitfalls in interpreting such data and models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that neural data alone is insufficient to infer the computational mechanisms of sentence processing, and that models must be evaluated based on cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles to be explanatory.
papers.conclusion: Computational modeling is vital for understanding sentence processing, but models must compute linguistically-sufficient representations via explicit cognitive operations and stay faithful to neurophysiological principles, and should not be judged solely on predictive power.
papers.key_findings:
The presence of a 1-2-4 Hz pattern in neural data does not necessarily imply hierarchical processing; it can also arise from associative models.
Artificial neural networks can produce the 1-2-4 Hz pattern without explicit sentence structure, but this does not rule out hierarchical processing in the brain.
Predictive power of a model is not the sole criterion for explaining brain function; models must also be faithful to cognitive and neural principles.
The amount of training data used in ANNs may not reflect the brain's learning environment, and rule-based models might be more explanatory in some cases.
Statistical models are not necessarily more parsimonious than hierarchical models, as they may require extensive training and latent syntactic information.
future_direction: Using naturalistic paradigms to study language processing
Integrating multiple data sources (e.g., EEG, fMRI) to test models
Developing models that are explicit about cognitive operations and neurophysiological implementation
papers.abstract: Sentences contain structure that determines their meaning beyond that of individual words. An influential study by Ding and colleagues (2016) used frequency tagging of phrases and sentences to show that the human brain is sensitive to structure by finding peaks of neural power at the rate at which structures were presented. Since then, there has been a rich debate on how to best explain this pattern of results with profound impact on the language sciences. Models that use hierarchical structure building, as well as models based on associative sequence processing, can predict the neural response, creating an inferential impasse as to which class of models explains the nature of the linguistic computations reflected in the neural readout. In the current manuscript, we discuss pitfalls and common fallacies seen in the conclusions drawn in the literature illustrated by various simulations. We conclude that inferring the neural operations of sentence processing based on these neural data, and any like it, alone, is insufficient. We discuss how to best evaluate models and how to approach the modeling of neural readouts to sentence processing in a manner that remains faithful to cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles.

papers.title: Multi-Scale Probabilistic Generation Theory: A Unified Information-Theoretic Framework for Hierarchical Structure in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do hierarchical structures emerge in large language models, and how do they vary across different architectures?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Multi-Scale Probabilistic Generation Theory (MSPGT), an information-theoretic framework modeling LLMs as Hierarchical Variational Information Bottleneck systems, and validates its predictions about multi-scale organization and architectural dependencies through experiments.
papers.conclusion: MSPGT advances interpretability from descriptive observation toward a predictive, information-theoretic understanding of how hierarchical structure emerges in LLMs, turning architectural differences into primary scientific observables.
papers.key_findings:
All tested models exhibit distinct multi-scale internal organization (Global, Intermediate, Local), but boundary positions and sensitivities vary significantly with architecture.
The Local-Intermediate boundary is highly stable within architecture families, while the Intermediate-Global boundary is sensitive to training dynamics and varies across families.
The intermediate scale is functionally conserved for structural control, as perturbations to it cause maximal structural degradation.
Local scale brittleness varies by orders of magnitude across architectures, with Llama models showing extreme sensitivity compared to Qwen.
The theory's predictions about intra-family boundary convergence and architecture-specific effects are strongly validated by the experimental results.
papers.limitation:
The theory abstracts away many architectural and optimization details (e.g., attention sparsity, tokenization effects, learning-rate schedules) that may influence information dynamics.
Experimental validation is restricted to four mid-sized open-weight models (7B–8B parameters) and English corpora; extending to multilingual and multimodal settings may reveal different scaling behaviors.
The estimation of compression coefficients and boundary locations relies on proxy measures (e.g., representational similarity, probe decodability, attention drift) which are not exact information-theoretic quantities.
The framework captures static hierarchical organization but not temporal adaptation during training or inference.
future_direction: Integrate dynamic training trajectories to study how hierarchical structure evolves during optimization.
Extend the analysis to cross-architecture scaling laws and broader model families.
Test and refine the predictive scope of the theory in multilingual and multimodal settings.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable emergent abilities but remain poorly understood at a mechanistic level. This paper introduces the Multi-Scale Probabilistic Generation Theory (MSPGT), a theoretical framework that models LLMs as Hierarchical Variational Information Bottleneck (H-VIB) systems. MSPGT posits that standard language modeling objectives implicitly optimize multi-scale information compression, leading to the spontaneous formation of three internal processing scales-Global, Intermediate, and Local. We formalize this principle, derive falsifiable predictions about boundary positions and architectural dependencies, and validate them through cross-model experiments combining multi-signal fusion and causal interventions. Results across Llama and Qwen families reveal consistent multi-scale organization but strong architecture-specific variations, partially supporting and refining the theory. MSPGT thus advances interpretability from descriptive observation toward predictive, information-theoretic understanding of how hierarchical structure emerges within large neural language models.

papers.title: An Analysis of Encoder Representations in Transformer-Based Machine Translation
papers.research_question: What kind of linguistic information (syntactic and semantic) is learned by the encoder of Transformer-based machine translation models, and how does it vary across layers and models with different translation quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes encoder representations in Transformer-based machine translation and finds that specific attention heads capture syntactic dependencies, with lower layers encoding more syntax and higher layers more semantics.
papers.conclusion: The experimental evaluation sheds light on interesting findings about dependency relations and syntactic and semantic behavior across layers in Transformer encoder representations.
papers.key_findings:
Each layer has at least one attention head that encodes a significant amount of syntactic dependencies.
Lower layers tend to encode more syntactic information, while upper layers move towards semantic tasks.
The information about the length of the input sentence starts to vanish after the third layer.
Attention can be used to transfer knowledge between high- and low-resource languages, improving translation quality.
future_direction: Extend the analysis with probing tasks to evaluate other linguistic properties.
Use a recent evaluation dataset for analysis.
Analyze the attention weights between the encoder and the decoder.
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism is a successful technique in modern NLP, especially in tasks like machine translation. The recently proposed network architecture of the Transformer is based entirely on attention mechanisms and achieves new state of the art results in neural machine translation, outperforming other sequence-to-sequence models. However, so far not much is known about the internal properties of the model and the representations it learns to achieve that performance. To study this question, we investigate the information that is learned by the attention mechanism in Transformer models with different translation quality. We assess the representations of the encoder by extracting dependency relations based on self-attention weights, we perform four probing tasks to study the amount of syntactic and semantic captured information and we also test attention in a transfer learning scenario. Our analysis sheds light on the relative strengths and weaknesses of the various encoder representations. We observe that specific attention heads mark syntactic dependency relations and we can also confirm that lower layers tend to learn more about syntax while higher layers tend to encode more semantics.

papers.title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes positional information in lower layers and switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. The paper also introduces a 'confusion score' to quantify intrusion effects in BERT's self-attention mechanism.
papers.conclusion: BERT composes increasingly abstract hierarchical representations of linguistic structure using self-attention, but does not show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure found in human processing.
papers.key_findings:
Diagnostic classifiers show BERT's lower layers encode positional information well, while higher layers encode hierarchical information.
The proposed confusion score reveals BERT's attention is sensitive to syntactic structure and grammatical features (number, gender) in subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora.
BERT's attention is not perfectly syntactic; it sometimes attends to grammatically inaccessible or mismatched distractors.
Confusion scores decrease with layer depth, and there is an increase in confusion at layer 4, coinciding with the degradation of positional information.
BERT's performance on possessive constructions in the subject noun task is poor, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
papers.limitation:
BERT performed poorly on possessive constructions in the subject noun task, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
BERT's attention is only incompletely modulated by structural and featural properties, and attention is sometimes spread across grammatically irrelevant elements.
future_direction: Investigate or visualize layer-on-layer changes in BERT’s structural and positional information, particularly between layers 3 and 4.
Retrieve the increasingly hierarchical representations of BERT across layers via the self-attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT's representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT's representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT's representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

papers.title: Entropy-Lens: Uncovering Decision Strategies in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do token prediction dynamics (expansion and pruning strategies) in LLMs vary across model families, tasks, and output formats, and how do these strategies impact downstream performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Entropy-Lens, a method to distill token-space dynamics of the residual stream into low-dimensional entropy profiles, revealing family-specific, task-specific, and format-specific patterns in expansion and pruning strategies, with expansion usually being more critical for performance.
papers.conclusion: Entropy-Lens provides a low-dimensional, interpretable view of token prediction dynamics in LLMs, revealing systematic patterns in how models expand and prune candidate tokens, which are informative about model family, task, and format, thereby enhancing understanding of information processing across model depth.
papers.key_findings:
Entropy profiles are family-specific and invariant under depth rescaling, showing that larger models refine the same underlying decision process.
Entropy profiles are characteristic of task type (generative, syntactic, semantic) and output format (poem, scientific piece, chat log).
Expansion and pruning strategies have unequal impact on downstream performance, with the expansion strategy usually being more critical for maintaining accuracy.
Entropy profiles can distinguish between correct and incorrect answers in multiple-choice question answering (MMLU).
The method is model-agnostic and works across a wide range of model families and sizes without requiring gradients, fine-tuning, or auxiliary probes.
papers.limitation:
Lack of mechanistic understanding of which specific architectural components or training schemes play a causal role in shaping a particular entropy profile.
Unclear how different training stages (e.g., fine-tuning, RLHF) alter the relative importance of expansion and pruning phases for downstream performance.
Analysis confined to decoder-only Transformers; not yet extended to architectures with different information flow paradigms, such as ViTs or Mixture-of-Experts.
future_direction: Mechanistic understanding of which architectural components or training schemes cause specific entropy profiles.
Investigating how different training stages alter the relative importance of expansion and pruning strategies.
Extending the framework to other architectures such as Vision Transformers (ViTs) or Mixture-of-Experts models.
papers.abstract: In large language models (LLMs), each block operates on the residual stream to map input token sequences to output token distributions. However, most of the interpretability literature focuses on internal latent representations, leaving token-space dynamics underexplored. The high dimensionality and categoricity of token distributions hinder their analysis, as standard statistical descriptors are not suitable. We show that the entropy of logit-lens predictions overcomes these issues. In doing so, it provides a per-layer scalar, permutation-invariant metric. We introduce Entropy-Lens to distill the token-space dynamics of the residual stream into a low-dimensional signal. We call this signal the entropy profile. We apply our method to a variety of model sizes and families, showing that (i) entropy profiles uncover token prediction dynamics driven by expansion and pruning strategies; (ii) these dynamics are family-specific and invariant under depth rescaling; (iii) they are characteristic of task type and output format; (iv) these strategies have unequal impact on downstream performance, with the expansion strategy usually being more critical. Ultimately, our findings further enhance our understanding of the residual stream, enabling a granular assessment of how information is processed across model depth.

papers.title: Contextual Feature Extraction Hierarchies Converge in Large Language Models and the Brain
papers.research_question: What factors contribute to the alignment of large language models (LLMs) with the brain's language processing mechanisms, and do LLMs share fundamental computational principles that increasingly align with the spoken language processing pathway in the human brain?
papers.core_contribution: The study finds that higher-performing large language models (LLMs) exhibit greater alignment with the brain's hierarchical language processing, and that contextual information is a key factor driving this convergence.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal that hierarchical structure and contextual dependencies are fundamental to language processing, leading to convergent strategies in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Higher-performing LLMs achieve higher peak brain similarity scores.
Better-performing LLMs peak in brain similarity at earlier layers compared to lower-performing models.
Better-performing LLMs have hierarchical feature extraction pathways that more closely align with the brain's hierarchy.
Contextual information is crucial for brain similarity and hierarchy alignment, with long context windows being particularly important.
Top-performing LLMs converge in their feature extraction hierarchies, as shown by high inter-model similarity.
papers.limitation:
Limited iEEG coverage may not capture all relevant brain regions.
The speech comprehension task is simple and may not fully engage higher-level language processing.
LLMs are trained for next-word prediction, which differs from the comprehension task performed by subjects.
future_direction: Using brain similarity as an evaluation metric for LLM development.
Improving contextual processing in LLMs to enhance performance and brain alignment.
Investigating the role of later layers in LLMs for higher-order integration.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence have sparked interest in the parallels between large language models (LLMs) and human neural processing, particularly in language comprehension. While prior research has established similarities in the representation of LLMs and the brain, the underlying computational principles that cause this convergence, especially in the context of evolving LLMs, remain elusive. Here, we examined a diverse selection of high-performance LLMs with similar parameter sizes to investigate the factors contributing to their alignment with the brain's language processing mechanisms. We find that as LLMs achieve higher performance on benchmark tasks, they not only become more brain-like as measured by higher performance when predicting neural responses from LLM embeddings, but also their hierarchical feature extraction pathways map more closely onto the brain's while using fewer layers to do the same encoding. We also compare the feature extraction pathways of the LLMs to each other and identify new ways in which high-performing models have converged toward similar hierarchical processing mechanisms. Finally, we show the importance of contextual information in improving model performance and brain similarity. Our findings reveal the converging aspects of language processing in the brain and LLMs and offer new directions for developing models that align more closely with human cognitive processing.

papers.title: Roles and Utilization of Attention Heads in Transformer-based Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are basic linguistic properties captured with the attention heads across transformer-based models and used for downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an analysis method to understand where linguistic properties are learned and represented in attention heads of transformer architectures, and shows that selecting and concatenating influential attention heads can improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that understanding the roles of attention heads can lead to adaptive sentence representations that improve downstream task performance, and reveals internal behaviors of transformer models during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Different attention heads on different layers are specialized for different linguistic properties (syntactic, semantic, surface).
The last layer of transformer encoders is not always the best for representing linguistic properties; earlier layers often dominate.
Concatenating the outputs of the top-n influential attention heads (selected via probing) yields better sentence representations and improves downstream task performance.
During fine-tuning, the initial superior attention heads remain influential and their performance is amplified, while adjacent heads also show increased performance.
Attention heads handle both syntactic and semantic information in a balanced way, with a linear relationship between their syntactic and semantic scores.
future_direction: Investigation of how heat maps vary during extensive pre-training to understand the dynamics of the learning processes.
papers.abstract: Sentence encoders based on the transformer architecture have shown promising results on various natural language tasks. The main impetus lies in the pre-trained neural language models that capture long-range dependencies among words, owing to multi-head attention that is unique in the architecture. However, little is known for how linguistic properties are processed, represented, and utilized for downstream tasks among hundreds of attention heads inside the pre-trained transformerbased model. For the initial goal of examining the roles of attention heads in handling a set of linguistic features, we conducted a set of experiments with ten probing tasks and three downstream tasks on four pre-trained transformer families (GPT, GPT2, BERT, and ELECTRA). Meaningful insights are shown through the lens of heat map visualization and utilized to propose a relatively simple sentence representation method that takes advantage of most influential attention heads, resulting in additional performance improvements on the downstream tasks.

papers.title: Structural Persistence in Language Models: Priming as a Window into Abstract Language Representations
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether modern neural language models exhibit structural priming, what factors influence the priming effect, and the nature of the structural representations they acquire.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer language models exhibit structural priming, indicating they encode abstract structural information, and that this priming is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, with evidence for hierarchical syntactic representations.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that Transformer language models are susceptible to structural priming, revealing they encode abstract structural information that is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, and may involve hierarchical syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer language models show evidence of structural priming.
Priming strength is boosted by semantic similarity and lexical overlap between prime and target sentences.
Priming effects persist but are asymmetrical when primes are semantically implausible.
Priming strength increases with recency (proximity) and cumulative exposure to the prime structure.
The structural representations may encode hierarchical syntactic information, as shown by priming with nested dependencies.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on only two syntactic alternations in English.
The corpus is template-based and may not capture naturalistic language.
Only auto-regressive language models are considered; masked LMs are not investigated.
future_direction: Extend the investigation to other syntactic constructions and languages.
Use more naturalistic data beyond template-based corpora.
Investigate structural priming in masked language models.
papers.abstract: Abstract We investigate the extent to which modern neural language models are susceptible to structural priming, the phenomenon whereby the structure of a sentence makes the same structure more probable in a follow-up sentence. We explore how priming can be used to study the potential of these models to learn abstract structural information, which is a prerequisite for good performance on tasks that require natural language understanding skills. We introduce a novel metric and release Prime-LM, a large corpus where we control for various linguistic factors that interact with priming strength. We find that Transformer models indeed show evidence of structural priming, but also that the generalizations they learned are to some extent modulated by semantic information. Our experiments also show that the representations acquired by the models may not only encode abstract sequential structure but involve certain level of hierarchical syntactic information. More generally, our study shows that the priming paradigm is a useful, additional tool for gaining insights into the capacities of language models and opens the door to future priming-based investigations that probe the model’s internal states.1

papers.title: Representations as Language: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Interpretability
papers.research_question: What systematic structures emerge in the representations learned by transformers, and how do they relate to generalization and training dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an information-theoretic framework for interpretability that quantifies structure in representations, identifies two phases of training, and shows how representational structure relates to generalization and model size.
papers.conclusion: The linguistically-motivated approach helps characterize training dynamics and explain generalization, and suggests that intuitions from linguistics and cognitive science about good representations transfer to deep learning models.
papers.key_findings:
Two distinct phases of training: an initial phase of in-distribution learning where representations align with token and part-of-speech information, and a second phase where representations become robust to noise and compress.
Generalization performance improves during the second phase, linking generalization to robustness to noise.
Larger models compress their representations more than smaller models.
The proposed measures (information, variation, regularity, disentanglement) can predict which models will generalize best based on their representational structure.
papers.limitation:
Some results may be particular to the hyperparameters used for training.
The entropy estimation method is an approximation and makes minimal assumptions, but is invariant to linear transformations.
future_direction: Apply the analysis to large-scale translation tasks.
Extend the approach to other levels of abstraction and other models.
papers.abstract: Large scale neural models show impressive performance across a wide array of linguistic tasks. Despite this they remain, largely, black-boxes - inducing vector-representations of their input that prove difficult to interpret. This limits our ability to understand what they learn, and when the learn it, or describe what kinds of representations generalise well out of distribution. To address this we introduce a novel approach to interpretability that looks at the mapping a model learns from sentences to representations as a kind of language in its own right. In doing so we introduce a set of information-theoretic measures that quantify how structured a model's representations are with respect to its input, and when during training that structure arises. Our measures are fast to compute, grounded in linguistic theory, and can predict which models will generalise best based on their representations. We use these measures to describe two distinct phases of training a transformer: an initial phase of in-distribution learning which reduces task loss, then a second stage where representations becoming robust to noise. Generalisation performance begins to increase during this second phase, drawing a link between generalisation and robustness to noise. Finally we look at how model size affects the structure of the representational space, showing that larger models ultimately compress their representations more than their smaller counterparts.

papers.title: How is BERT surprised? Layerwise detection of linguistic anomalies
papers.research_question: Do transformer language models exhibit different surprisal patterns in intermediate layers for different types of linguistic anomalies (morphosyntactic, semantic, commonsense)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Gaussian model for density estimation at intermediate layers of language models to detect linguistic anomalies, revealing that morphosyntactic anomalies are detected earlier than semantic anomalies, and commonsense anomalies are not detected at any layer.
papers.conclusion: The experiments reveal that out-of-domain points in lower layers correspond to low-frequency tokens, while grammatically anomalous inputs are out-of-domain in higher layers. Furthermore, morphosyntactic anomalies are recognized as out-of-domain starting from lower layers compared to semantic anomalies, and commonsense anomalies do not generate out-of-domain embeddings at any layer, indicating that language models use different mechanisms for different anomaly types.
papers.key_findings:
Lower layer surprisal is highly correlated with token frequency, but this correlation diminishes in upper layers.
Morphosyntactic anomalies produce high surprisal in earlier layers (layers 3-4) compared to semantic anomalies (layers 9 and above).
Commonsense anomalies do not result in surprisals at any layer.
The Gaussian anomaly model is competitive with masked language model scoring on grammaticality judgement, especially for morphosyntactic tasks.
RoBERTa performs best among the three models, while XLNet performs poorly.
papers.limitation:
