papers.conclusion: Simple models may carry more statistical signal and less noise than transformer-based models, suggesting that combining the high accuracy of LLMs with equally plausible explanations as simpler models may require moving beyond word-level univariate first-order explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The signal of CamemBERT explanations decreases as the number of equivalent models increases, indicating flattened average attention maps.
The average signal of CamemBERT explanations is lower than that of the feature-based model for both raw and normalized explanations.
The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for CamemBERT is below one, meaning noise (variance due to training randomness) dominates signal (variance of mean attention across words).
Normalizing explanations to have non-zero weights on the same number of words reduces signal for both models but CamemBERT still exhibits lower signal.
Explanations from CamemBERT are more sensitive to training randomness compared to the feature-based model, which has no noise due to deterministic training.
papers.limitation:
The conclusion is based on a single classification task, so its generalizability to other datasets is uncertain.
The statistical definition of signal and noise may deviate from a more semantic definition of explanation informativeness.
future_direction: Investigate more complex explanations using t-tuples of words, d attention values per word, and higher-order statistics.
Assess whether human readers can understand such complex explanations.
Explore if the variance in explanations corresponds to variance in human viewpoints, similar to human annotator subjectivity.
papers.abstract: The explanations of large language models have recently been shown to be sensitive to the randomness used for their training, creating a need to characterize this sensitivity. In this paper, we propose a characterization that questions the possibility to provide simple and informative explanations for such models. To this end, we give statistical definitions for the explanations' signal, noise and signal-to-noise ratio. We highlight that, in a typical case study where word-level univariate explanations are analyzed with first-order statistical tools, the explanations of simple feature-based models carry more signal and less noise than those of transformer ones. We then discuss the possibility to improve these results with alternative definitions of signal and noise that would capture more complex explanations and analysis methods, while also questioning the tradeoff with their plausibility for readers.

papers.title: Linguistic Minimal Pairs Elicit Linguistic Similarity in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models represent different linguistic phenomena, and are linguistically similar phenomena represented similarly in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method using linguistic minimal pairs to measure linguistic similarity in LLMs, revealing that linguistic similarity is influenced by training data, aligns with fine-grained linguistic categories, weakly correlates with semantic similarity, and shows limited cross-lingual alignment.
papers.conclusion: The work provides insights into LLMs' internal language processing, bridging neural models and linguistic theory, and offers a foundation for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages.
Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones.
Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, indicating its context-dependent nature.
LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Dependent on the quality and scope of existing linguistic minimal pair datasets
Limited to three languages, not representing global linguistic diversity
Only captures a fraction of language's complexity with 150 phenomena
future_direction: Developing more high-quality minimal pairs
Broadening language coverage to include more diverse linguistic families
Increasing the range of phenomena studied
papers.abstract: We introduce a novel analysis that leverages linguistic minimal pairs to probe the internal linguistic representations of Large Language Models (LLMs). By measuring the similarity between LLM activation differences across minimal pairs, we quantify the and gain insight into the linguistic knowledge captured by LLMs. Our large-scale experiments, spanning 100+ LLMs and 150k minimal pairs in three languages, reveal properties of linguistic similarity from four key aspects: consistency across LLMs, relation to theoretical categorizations, dependency to semantic context, and cross-lingual alignment of relevant phenomena. Our findings suggest that 1) linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages. 2) Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones. 3) Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, showing its context-dependent nature. 4) LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena. This work demonstrates the potential of minimal pairs as a window into the neural representations of language in LLMs, shedding light on the relationship between LLMs and linguistic theory. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/ChenDelong1999/Linguistic-Similarity

papers.title: From Tokens to Words: On the Inner Lexicon of LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs encode words internally from sub-word tokens, and if so, how.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally detokenize sub-word tokens into whole-word representations in early to middle layers via an inner lexicon, enabling vocabulary expansion without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The work unravels the word detokenization process in LLMs, showing it occurs in early to middle layers and enables practical applications for optimizing tokenization and inference costs.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can distinguish words from nonwords, with the distinction emerging in early to middle layers.
The last token of a word (even if split) can be decoded as the full word, indicating an inner lexicon.
FFN layers are crucial for retrieving full-word representations from the inner lexicon.
Attention patterns show early layers aggregate sub-word tokens, then later layers ignore them as the full word representation forms.
The inner lexicon can be used to expand the model's vocabulary without fine-tuning, reducing token count and maintaining performance.
papers.limitation:
22.6% of multi-token words are never successfully decoded, indicating the inner lexicon does not cover all words.
Vocabulary expansion success rate is lower for morphologically rich languages like Arabic (16%).
papers.abstract: Natural language is composed of words, but modern large language models (LLMs) process sub-words as input. A natural question raised by this discrepancy is whether LLMs encode words internally, and if so how. We present evidence that LLMs engage in an intrinsic detokenization process, where sub-word sequences are combined into coherent whole-word representations at their last token. Our experiments show that this process primarily takes place within the early and middle layers of the model. We further demonstrate its robustness to arbitrary splits (e.g., "cats" to "ca" and "ts"), typos, and importantly-to out-of-vocabulary words: when feeding the last token internal representations of such words to the model as input, it can "understand" them as the complete word despite never seeing such representations as input during training. Our findings suggest that LLMs maintain a latent vocabulary beyond the tokenizer's scope. These insights provide a practical, finetuning-free application for expanding the vocabulary of pre-trained models. By enabling the addition of new vocabulary words, we reduce input length and inference iterations, which reduces both space and model latency, with little to no loss in model accuracy.

papers.title: What Happens During the Loss Plateau? Understanding Abrupt Learning in Transformers
papers.research_question: What common patterns manifest in the model's input-output behavior and internal representations during the extended loss plateau phase, and what critical changes precede the sudden shift towards higher performance?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies that during the loss plateau in Transformer training, models develop a partial solution, exhibit repetition bias and internal representation collapse, and that the slow learning of optimal attention maps is a key bottleneck driving these dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies repetition bias and representation collapse as key characteristics of early-phase implicit biases in Transformer training, closely connected to the loss plateau, and suggests a 'search' over sequence tokens as a possible cause.
papers.key_findings:
During the initial loss plateau, the model often learns a partial solution, correctly predicting a subset of easier tokens while failing on more complex parts.
A strong repetition bias appears in model outputs during the plateau, quantified by repetition frequency and sequence entropy.
Internal representation collapse occurs where hidden states for different tokens become nearly parallel (high cosine similarity).
Gradual learning of the optimal attention pattern commences during the plateau and precedes the sudden loss drop; intervening on attention maps alters plateau duration and degenerate behaviors.
The phenomena of repetition bias and representation collapse are also observed in the early pre-training stages of large language models like Pythia and OLMo.
future_direction: Understanding why behaviors such as representation collapse exist during early time training.
Rigorous theoretical validation of the 'search' hypothesis and how it connects to task complexity.
papers.abstract: Training Transformers on algorithmic tasks frequently demonstrates an intriguing abrupt learning phenomenon: an extended performance plateau followed by a sudden, sharp improvement. This work investigates the underlying mechanisms for such dynamics, primarily in shallow Transformers. We reveal that during the plateau, the model often develops an interpretable partial solution while simultaneously exhibiting a strong repetition bias in their outputs. This output degeneracy is accompanied by internal representation collapse, where hidden states across different tokens become nearly parallel. We further identify the slow learning of optimal attention maps as a key bottleneck. Hidden progress in attention configuration during the plateau precedes the eventual rapid convergence, and directly intervening on attention significantly alters plateau duration and the severity of repetition bias and representational collapse. We validate that these identified phenomena-repetition bias and representation collapse-are not artifacts of toy setups but also manifest in the early pre-training stage of large language models like Pythia and OLMo.

papers.title: Talking Heads: Understanding Inter-layer Communication in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How is information represented and routed between layers in transformer language models, specifically through low-rank communication channels?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs use low-rank subspaces (communication channels) in the residual stream to pass information between layers; these channels can be identified via SVD of weight matrices and are causally important for model behaviors.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn intricately structured representations through pretraining, and the discovered communication channels provide a mechanistic explanation for some prompt sensitivities, enabling improved model performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer LMs use low-rank (1D or 2D) subspaces in the residual stream for inter-layer communication.
These communication channels can be identified by applying SVD to weight matrices (OV and QK) and computing composition scores on the rank-1 components.
The identified channels are causally important for model behaviors, such as inhibition in the IOI task.
The model's sensitivity to item order in a list (Laundry List task) is explained by the limited capacity of these low-rank channels.
Model editing (zeroing or scaling components) based on these channels can significantly improve performance on the Laundry List task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not work for key composition (Appendix B).
Analysis is limited to two small models (GPT-2 small and Pythia 160m).
Difficulty in controlling all variables in the available data (Section 7).
future_direction: Future work in static weight analysis more generally.
More rigorous analysis of interactions between specific heads (e.g., 8.3 and 9.9).
Extending the method to analyze more complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: Although it is known that transformer language models (LMs) pass features from early layers to later layers, it is not well understood how this information is represented and routed by the model. We analyze a mechanism used in two LMs to selectively inhibit items in a context in one task, and find that it underlies a commonly used abstraction across many context-retrieval behaviors. Specifically, we find that models write into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream to represent features which are then read out by later layers, forming low-rank communication channels (Elhage et al., 2021) between layers. A particular 3D subspace in model activations in GPT-2 can be traversed to positionally index items in lists, and we show that this mechanism can explain an otherwise arbitrary-seeming sensitivity of the model to the order of items in the prompt. That is, the model has trouble copying the correct information from context when many items ``crowd" this limited space. By decomposing attention heads with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that previously described interactions between heads separated by one or more layers can be predicted via analysis of their weight matrices alone. We show that it is possible to manipulate the internal model representations as well as edit model weights based on the mechanism we discover in order to significantly improve performance on our synthetic Laundry List task, which requires recall from a list, often improving task accuracy by over 20%. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly intricate interpretable structure learned from language model pretraining, and helps us understand why sophisticated LMs sometimes fail in simple domains, facilitating future analysis of more complex behaviors.

papers.title: Blackbox meets blackbox: Representational Similarity and Stability Analysis of Neural Language Models and Brains
papers.research_question: How sensitive are neural language model representations to prior context, and how do these representations compare to human brain activations during story reading?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Representational Stability Analysis (ReStA) to analyze context-dependence in neural language models, finding that LSTM-based models are more similar to brain representations than transformer-based models, and that deeper layers are more context-dependent.
papers.conclusion: ReStA and RSA are useful for comparing models and brains, but caution is required due to low correlations. LSTM-based models are more similar to brain data, and brain data may only reflect shallow linguistic processing.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM-based models (GoogleLM and ELMO) show higher similarity between their two layers compared to BERT.
For LSTM-based models, the first layer is less sensitive to context length than the last layer, suggesting a hierarchical encoding mechanism.
Transformer-based models (BERT) are more sensitive to context length overall, and their first layer is more context-dependent than the last layer.
Among the models, UniSentEnc learns very different representations from the others, possibly due to different training objectives.
LSTM-based models achieve higher similarity with brain data compared to GloVe and transformer-based models, and their lower layers align better with brain representations.
papers.limitation:
Standard RSA assumes all features of the representational spaces have equal contributions, leading to information loss.
The representational similarity between all models and the brain images remains very low.
Inherent issues in the brain data (e.g., hemodynamic response delay, noise) and complexity of the story reading task make evaluation hard.
future_direction: Perform further analysis on various (bigger) datasets to better interpret what is happening in both the brain and computational models.
Postpone further analysis with the predictive approach (linear regression) to future studies.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we define and apply representational stability analysis (ReStA), an intuitive way of analyzing neural language models. ReStA is a variant of the popular representational similarity analysis (RSA) in cognitive neuroscience. While RSA can be used to compare representations in models, model components, and human brains, ReStA compares instances of the same model, while systematically varying single model parameter. Using ReStA, we study four recent and successful neural language models, and evaluate how sensitive their internal representations are to the amount of prior context. Using RSA, we perform a systematic study of how similar the representational spaces in the first and second (or higher) layers of these models are to each other and to patterns of activation in the human brain. Our results reveal surprisingly strong differences between language models, and give insights into where the deep linguistic processing, that integrates information over multiple sentences, is happening in these models. The combination of ReStA and RSA on models and brains allows us to start addressing the important question of what kind of linguistic processes we can hope to observe in fMRI brain imaging data. In particular, our results suggest that the data on story reading from Wehbe et al. (2014) contains a signal of shallow linguistic processing, but show no evidence on the more interesting deep linguistic processing.

papers.title: Transformers Are Born Biased: Structural Inductive Biases at Random Initialization and Their Practical Consequences
papers.research_question: Do randomly initialized transformers exhibit systematic structural biases, and what are their mechanisms and practical consequences?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers exhibit strong structural biases at random initialization due to representation contraction driven by MLP and attention, which persist through training and enable seed-specific fingerprinting (SeedPrint) and explain the attention-sink phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are not blank slates; they possess inherent structural biases at initialization that persist through training, with implications for model fingerprinting and architecture design.
papers.key_findings:
Randomly initialized transformers show extreme token preferences, with certain tokens predicted orders of magnitude more often than others.
This preference arises from inter-sequence representation contraction, where last-token representations from different sequences become highly similar.
The contraction is primarily driven by asymmetric nonlinear activations in MLP layers, and amplified by self-attention through intra-sequence aggregation.
These initialization-induced biases persist throughout training, forming a stable model identity that can be used for fingerprinting (SeedPrint).
The attention mechanism's intra-sequence contraction leads to a positional discrepancy that causally explains the attention-sink phenomenon in trained LLMs.
future_direction: Design architectures that are more neutral or explicitly incorporate desired inductive biases.
Treat initialization choices as hyperparameters tuned for final model behavior, not just optimization stability.
Extend the fingerprinting method to more challenging scenarios, such as detecting obfuscated or distilled models.
papers.abstract: Transformers underpin modern large language models (LLMs) and are commonly assumed to be behaviorally unstructured at random initialization, with all meaningful preferences emerging only through large-scale training. We challenge this assumption by showing that randomly initialized transformers already exhibit strong and systematic structural biases. In particular, untrained models display extreme token preferences: across random input sequences, certain tokens are predicted with probabilities orders of magnitude larger. We provide a mechanistic explanation for this phenomenon by dissecting the transformer architecture at initialization. We show that extreme token preference arises from a contraction of token representations along a random seed-dependent direction. This contraction is driven by two interacting forces: (i) asymmetric nonlinear activations in MLP sublayers induce global (inter-sequence) representation concentration, and (ii) self-attention further amplifies this effect through local (intra-sequence) aggregation. Together, these mechanisms align hidden representations along a direction determined solely by the random initialization, producing highly non-uniform next-token predictions. Beyond mechanistic insight, we demonstrate that these initialization-induced biases persist throughout training, forming a stable and intrinsic model identity. Leveraging this property, we introduce SeedPrint, a fingerprinting method that can reliably distinguish models that differ only in their random initialization, even after extensive training and under substantial distribution shift. Finally, we identify a fundamental positional discrepancy inherent to the attention mechanism's intra-sequence contraction that is causally linked to the attention-sink phenomenon. This discovery provides a principled explanation for the emergence of sinks and offers a pathway for their control.

papers.title: Superscopes: Amplifying Internal Feature Representations for Language Model Interpretation
papers.research_question: How can we interpret internal representations (like MLP outputs and hidden states) in language models that are not interpretable with existing self-interpretation methods, by amplifying weak features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Superscopes, a method that amplifies weak features in internal representations (MLP outputs and hidden states) to enable their interpretation via self-interpretation methods like Patchscopes, without requiring additional training.
papers.conclusion: Superscopes extends Patchscopes by amplifying internal representations, enabling interpretation of previously uninterpretable MLP outputs and hidden states, and draws a parallel to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models.
papers.key_findings:
Amplifying MLP outputs reveals meaningful interpretations that are not accessible with standard Patchscopes.
Amplifying hidden states can reveal interpretations in layers before contextualization occurs.
The amplification technique is analogous to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models, as both amplify directional shifts.
The Superscopes framework can automatically identify optimal amplification factors for interpretation.
The method demonstrates that weak features in internal representations can be amplified to reveal semantic content.
papers.limitation:
The method does not currently handle attention outputs, which may have a denser superposition of features.
The method for selecting the optimal amplifier may not be fully effective and could be improved.
future_direction: Extracting meaning from attention outputs.
Developing more effective approaches for selecting the optimal amplifier.
Exploring alternative ways to amplify meaning within Superscopes, such as using a different base vector for patching.
papers.abstract: Understanding and interpreting the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains an open challenge. Patchscopes introduced a method for probing internal activations by patching them into new prompts, prompting models to self-explain their hidden representations. We introduce Superscopes, a technique that systematically amplifies superposed features in MLP outputs (multilayer perceptron) and hidden states before patching them into new contexts. Inspired by the "features as directions" perspective and the Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) approach from diffusion models, Superscopes amplifies weak but meaningful features, enabling the interpretation of internal representations that previous methods failed to explain-all without requiring additional training. This approach provides new insights into how LLMs build context and represent complex concepts, further advancing mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: LogiDynamics: Unraveling the Dynamics of Inductive, Abductive and Deductive Logical Inferences in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: When and how can System 1 and System 2 logical inference pipelines be effectively leveraged to enhance LLM reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically investigates the comparative dynamics of System 1 (inductive) and System 2 (abductive/deductive) logical inference in LLMs, providing guidelines for when to use each and showing that advanced System 2 strategies can scale up reasoning.
papers.conclusion: This study offers foundational insights and actionable guidelines for strategically deploying logical inference to enhance LLM reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
System 2 pipelines generally excel, particularly in visual/symbolic modalities and harder tasks, while System 1 is competitive for textual and easier problems.
Task format significantly influences their relative advantage, with System 1 sometimes outperforming System 2 in free-text rule-execution.
Advanced System 2 strategies like hypothesis selection and iterative refinement can substantially scale LLM reasoning.
The findings generalize to broader in-context learning tasks where the input-output function is explicitly defined.
papers.limitation:
The precise generation of complex rules is challenging for most LLMs, leading to poor pattern inference accuracy in free-text generation.
Lengthy rationales in System 2 pipelines disrupt the well-structured few-shot patterns essential for in-context learning, impairing free-text generation precision.
The effectiveness of hypothesis refinement depends on the model's verification quality and the format of the hypothesis (e.g., Python code vs. free text).
papers.abstract: Tianshi Zheng, Cheng Jiayang, Chunyang Li, Haochen Shi, Zihao Wang, Jiaxin Bai, Yangqiu Song, Ginny Wong, Simon See. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2025.

papers.title: Moving Beyond Next-Token Prediction: Transformers are Context-Sensitive Language Generators
papers.research_question: How can Transformers be understood as stochastic approximations of left context-sensitive languages, bridging formal language theory and their generative power?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reframes Transformers as stochastic approximations of left context-sensitive languages, providing a formal language theory perspective that explains their human-like generative power.
papers.conclusion: Transformers stochastically approximate context-sensitive languages, bridging the gap between formal language theory and their practical generative power, and laying a foundation for future generative AI theory and applications.
papers.key_findings:
Next-token prediction in Transformers can be interpreted as probabilistic, dynamic approximations of left context-sensitive language (CSL) production rules.
Autoregressive generation in Transformers can be reinterpreted through the lens of formal language theory, specifically as derivations of left CSLs.
Transformers function as stochastic approximations of context-sensitive languages, which are widely recognized as models of human-like intelligence.
future_direction: Exploring expansions to general forms of context-sensitive grammars within autoregressive generation for improvements in performance and computational resource utilization.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), powered by Transformers, have demonstrated human-like intelligence capabilities, yet their underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This paper presents a novel framework for interpreting LLMs as probabilistic left context-sensitive languages (CSLs) generators. We hypothesize that Transformers can be effectively decomposed into three fundamental components: context windows, attention mechanisms, and autoregressive generation frameworks. This decomposition allows for the development of more flexible and interpretable computational models, moving beyond the traditional view of attention and autoregression as inseparable processes. We argue that next-token predictions can be understood as probabilistic, dynamic approximations of left CSL production rules, providing an intuitive explanation for how simple token predictions can yield human-like intelligence outputs. Given that all CSLs are left context-sensitive (Penttonen, 1974), we conclude that Transformers stochastically approximate CSLs, which are widely recognized as models of human-like intelligence. This interpretation bridges the gap between Formal Language Theory and the observed generative power of Transformers, laying a foundation for future advancements in generative AI theory and applications. Our novel perspective on Transformer architectures will foster a deeper understanding of LLMs and their future potentials.

papers.title: What Do Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn?
papers.research_question: What do self-supervised vision transformers learn? Specifically, how and why contrastive learning (CL) and masked image modeling (MIM) differ in their representations and downstream task performance.
papers.core_contribution: CL and MIM learn complementary representations: CL captures global shape information but suffers from attention collapse, while MIM captures local texture information and preserves diversity. A simple linear combination of both losses can outperform each individually.
papers.conclusion: CL and MIM have opposing properties and are complementary; combining them can improve performance, and even a simple harmonization method shows benefits.
papers.key_findings:
CL trains self-attentions to capture global patterns and object shapes, but leads to attention collapse into homogeneity, reducing representation diversity.
MIM focuses on local patterns and textures, preserving token-level diversity and excelling in fine-tuning and dense prediction tasks.
CL utilizes low-frequency signals (shape-biased), while MIM utilizes high-frequency signals (texture-biased).
CL plays a crucial role in later layers, while MIM is important in early layers.
A simple linear combination of CL and MIM objectives can leverage the advantages of both methods, improving performance in linear probing and fine-tuning.
future_direction: Exploring better ways to combine CL and MIM than linear combination, such as applying CL in later layers and MIM in early layers.
Extending findings to multi-stage Vision Transformers like PiT and Swin.
Enhancing individual properties of CL and MIM to improve shape or texture learning.
papers.abstract: We present a comparative study on how and why contrastive learning (CL) and masked image modeling (MIM) differ in their representations and in their performance of downstream tasks. In particular, we demonstrate that self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs) have the following properties: (1) CL trains self-attentions to capture longer-range global patterns than MIM, such as the shape of an object, especially in the later layers of the ViT architecture. This CL property helps ViTs linearly separate images in their representation spaces. However, it also makes the self-attentions collapse into homogeneity for all query tokens and heads. Such homogeneity of self-attention reduces the diversity of representations, worsening scalability and dense prediction performance. (2) CL utilizes the low-frequency signals of the representations, but MIM utilizes high-frequencies. Since low- and high-frequency information respectively represent shapes and textures, CL is more shape-oriented and MIM more texture-oriented. (3) CL plays a crucial role in the later layers, while MIM mainly focuses on the early layers. Upon these analyses, we find that CL and MIM can complement each other and observe that even the simplest harmonization can help leverage the advantages of both methods. The code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/cl-vs-mim.

papers.title: Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings Still Learn Positional Information
papers.research_question: Can transformer language models learn positional information without explicit positional encodings, and how do they do it?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer language models without explicit positional encodings (NoPos) can learn implicit positional information and achieve competitive performance, and this ability is due to the causal attention mask.
papers.conclusion: Transformer language models can learn positional information without explicit encodings, and this phenomenon is robust across settings but does not extend to masked language models, with the causal attention mechanism being the key factor.
papers.key_findings:
NoPos models achieve competitive perplexity compared to models with explicit positional encodings across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.
Probing experiments show that NoPos models learn an implicit notion of absolute positions in their hidden representations, similar to models with learned positional embeddings.
The success of NoPos models is unique to causal language models; masked language models fail to converge without positional encodings.
Shuffling the prefix tokens leads to a dramatic increase in loss, indicating that the model uses the learned positional information.
The causal attention mask is conjectured to allow the model to infer absolute positions by counting the number of attendable tokens.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models up to 1.3B parameters, and while the trend suggests the findings should hold for larger models, this is not tested.
NoPos models are always slightly worse than models with positional encodings, indicating that the inductive bias of positional encoding is important.
papers.abstract: Causal transformer language models (LMs), such as GPT-3, typically require some form of positional encoding, such as positional embeddings. However, we show that LMs without any explicit positional encoding are still competitive with standard models and that this phenomenon is robust across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.Probing experiments reveal that such models acquire an implicit notion of absolute positions throughout the network, effectively compensating for the missing information.We conjecture that causal attention enables the model to infer the number of predecessors that each token can attend to, thereby approximating its absolute position.Our findings indicate that causal LMs might derive positional awareness not only from the explicit positioning mechanism but also from the effects of the causal mask.

papers.title: Dimensionality and Ramping: Signatures of Sentence Integration in the Dynamics of Brains and Deep Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the neural vector code signatures of semantic composition during sentence comprehension? Specifically, does the intrinsic dimensionality of neural representations increase as a sentence unfolds, and are there specific dynamic patterns (phasic, ramping, sentence-final) associated with semantic integration?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that the intrinsic dimensionality of neural representations increases for meaningful sentences compared to Jabberwocky in both deep language models and human brain data. It also identifies three distinct dynamic patterns (phasic, ramping, and sentence-final) in the brain's processing of semantic composition.
papers.conclusion: The results provide a first glimpse into the neural geometry of semantic integration, showing that meaningful sentence composition is associated with increased representational dimensionality and specific, regionally specialized dynamic patterns in the brain, which are also partially mirrored in artificial neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Intrinsic dimensionality is higher for normal sentences than for Jabberwocky sentences in both human brain signals (sEEG/MEG) and in deep language models (LSTMs and Transformers).
Multivariate decoding reveals three superimposed temporal patterns when distinguishing normal from Jabberwocky sentences: a phasic pattern after each word, a ramping pattern that increases over the sentence, and a sentence-final pattern after the last word.
The ramping pattern becomes more pronounced in deeper layers of the language models.
The three dynamic patterns are associated with distinct brain regions: phasic patterns in temporal and parietal areas, ramping patterns in bilateral inferior and middle frontal gyri, and sentence-final patterns in left superior frontal gyrus and right orbitofrontal cortex.
Untrained language models do not show the same increase in intrinsic dimensionality for normal vs. Jabberwocky sentences, suggesting the effect emerges from linguistic training.
papers.abstract: A sentence is more than the sum of its words: its meaning depends on how they combine with one another. The brain mechanisms underlying such semantic composition remain poorly understood. To shed light on the neural vector code underlying semantic composition, we introduce two hypotheses: (1) the intrinsic dimensionality of the space of neural representations should increase as a sentence unfolds, paralleling the growing complexity of its semantic representation; and (2) this progressive integration should be reflected in ramping and sentence-final signals. To test these predictions, we designed a dataset of closely matched normal and jabberwocky sentences (composed of meaningless pseudo words) and displayed them to deep language models and to 11 human participants (5 men and 6 women) monitored with simultaneous MEG and intracranial EEG. In both deep language models and electrophysiological data, we found that representational dimensionality was higher for meaningful sentences than jabberwocky. Furthermore, multivariate decoding of normal versus jabberwocky confirmed three dynamic patterns: (1) a phasic pattern following each word, peaking in temporal and parietal areas; (2) a ramping pattern, characteristic of bilateral inferior and middle frontal gyri; and (3) a sentence-final pattern in left superior frontal gyrus and right orbitofrontal cortex. These results provide a first glimpse into the neural geometry of semantic integration and constrain the search for a neural code of linguistic composition. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT Starting from general linguistic concepts, we make two sets of predictions in neural signals evoked by reading multiword sentences. First, the intrinsic dimensionality of the representation should grow with additional meaningful words. Second, the neural dynamics should exhibit signatures of encoding, maintaining, and resolving semantic composition. We successfully validated these hypotheses in deep neural language models, artificial neural networks trained on text and performing very well on many natural language processing tasks. Then, using a unique combination of MEG and intracranial electrodes, we recorded high-resolution brain data from human participants while they read a controlled set of sentences. Time-resolved dimensionality analysis showed increasing dimensionality with meaning, and multivariate decoding allowed us to isolate the three dynamical patterns we had hypothesized.

papers.title: Does injecting linguistic structure into language models lead to better alignment with brain recordings?
papers.research_question: Does injecting linguistic structure into language models lead to better alignment with brain recordings?
papers.core_contribution: Injecting linguistic structure bias into language models via guided attention during fine-tuning can improve alignment with brain recordings, particularly for word-level fMRI data.
papers.conclusion: Injecting linguistic structure bias through guided attention can improve brain decoding performance, with clearer benefits for finer-grained (word-level) analyses, and highlights the importance of controlling for domain effects.
papers.key_findings:
For the word-level Wehbe2014 fMRI dataset, guided attention models significantly outperform pretrained and domain-finetuned baselines in brain decoding.
For the sentence-level Pereira2018 dataset, improvements are more modest, with UD and DM guided attention models showing some improvement over the pretrained baseline.
Domain of the fine-tuning data is an important confound affecting brain alignment; simply fine-tuning on a different domain can reduce alignment.
Guided attention models perform better on subject-verb agreement syntactic probing tasks, with performance ranking corresponding to brain decoding scores.
Guided attention improves performance on a semantic tagging task for most semantic categories, especially discourse and temporal relations.
papers.limitation:
The fMRI data was recorded during passive reading without a specific task, which may limit the ability to uncover fine-grained patterns of linguistic structure.
Potential confounds such as domain, corpus size, and dependency length differences between the linguistic formalisms are not fully controlled for due to the lack of a common annotated corpus.
future_direction: Investigating brain alignment using continuous, naturalistic listening fMRI datasets.
Using a common annotated corpus for all formalisms to properly control for confounds like domain and corpus size.
papers.abstract: Neuroscientists evaluate deep neural networks for natural language processing as possible candidate models for how language is processed in the brain. These models are often trained without explicit linguistic supervision, but have been shown to learn some linguistic structure in the absence of such supervision (Manning et al., 2020), potentially questioning the relevance of symbolic linguistic theories in modeling such cognitive processes (Warstadt and Bowman, 2020). We evaluate across two fMRI datasets whether language models align better with brain recordings, if their attention is biased by annotations from syntactic or semantic formalisms. Using structure from dependency or minimal recursion semantic annotations, we find alignments improve significantly for one of the datasets. For another dataset, we see more mixed results. We present an extensive analysis of these results. Our proposed approach enables the evaluation of more targeted hypotheses about the composition of meaning in the brain, expanding the range of possible scientific inferences a neuroscientist could make, and opens up new opportunities for cross-pollination between computational neuroscience and linguistics.

papers.title: Effects of Parameter Norm Growth During Transformer Training: Inductive Bias from Gradient Descent
papers.research_question: What are the effects of parameter norm growth during transformer training on the network's representations and inductive bias?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that parameter norm growth during transformer training leads to saturation, which characterizes an inductive bias of gradient descent and explains the emergent representations in attention heads.
papers.conclusion: The paper empirically found that parameter norm grows ∝ √t during T5 pretraining, likely due to approximate homogeneity, proved that norm growth induces saturation, and showed that pretrained transformers become approximately saturated, with attention heads splitting into argmax and mean behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Parameter norm grows proportionally to √t during T5 pretraining.
Norm growth induces saturation, where the network approximates a discretized network with saturated activation functions.
Pretrained transformers (T5, XLNet, etc.) show high saturation levels compared to randomly initialized ones.
Saturated attention heads exhibit two types: argmax (attending to few positions) and mean (attending uniformly).
The dynamics of norm growth can be explained by approximate homogeneity of transformers and misaligned gradients.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis assumes uniform norm growth across all parameters, which may not always hold.
future_direction: Future works are encouraged to track norm growth metrics during pretraining of new transformer language models.
The investigation of the function of attention heads that lie between argmax and mean modes is deferred to future work.
Developing a more complete theoretical story for weight decay and norm growth is left for future work.
papers.abstract: The capacity of neural networks like the widely adopted transformer is known to be very high. Evidence is emerging that they learn successfully due to inductive bias in the training routine, typically a variant of gradient descent (GD). To better understand this bias, we study the tendency for transformer parameters to grow in magnitude ( 2 norm) during training, and its implications for the emergent representations within self attention layers. Empirically, we document norm growth in the training of transformer language models, including T5 during its pretraining. As the parameters grow in magnitude, we prove that the network approximates a discretized network with saturated activation functions. Such "saturated" networks are known to have a reduced capacity compared to the full network family that can be described in terms of formal languages and automata. Our results suggest saturation is a new characterization of an inductive bias implicit in GD of particular interest for NLP. We leverage the emergent discrete structure in a saturated transformer to analyze the role of different attention heads, finding that some focus locally on a small number of positions, while other heads compute global averages, allowing counting. We believe understanding the interplay between these two capabilities may shed further light on the structure of computation within large transformers.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformers Models
papers.research_question: How to interactively explore and understand what attention heads in transformer models have learned, specifically in BERT, by combining attention visualization with nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to explore and explain learned representations and attention mechanisms in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to reveal intelligible structure in learned representations of transformer models, demonstrated with BERT on the Wizard of Oz corpus.
papers.key_findings:
At early layers (e.g., layer 1), masked token embeddings show similarity to common tokens like punctuation and determinants, with no meaningful linguistic information encoded.
As layers progress, more part-of-speech information is added; by layer 6, BERT becomes confident that a masked token is a verb, refining this estimation in later layers.
Complex dependencies such as direct object (DOBJ) are detected in early-middle layers but rely on a combination of multiple attention heads, not individual heads.
Positional heads attend to succeeding or preceding tokens and encode linguistic information about the attended-to word, such as part-of-speech and dependency relations.
EXBERT enables interactive exploration of how attention heads contribute to encoding linguistic features in token embeddings through nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.abstract: Large language models can produce powerful contextual representations that lead to improvements across many NLP tasks. Since these models are typically guided by a sequence of learned self attention mechanisms and may comprise undesired inductive biases, it is paramount to be able to explore what the attention has learned. While static analyses of these models lead to targeted insights, interactive tools are more dynamic and can help humans better gain an intuition for the model-internal reasoning process. We present exBERT, an interactive tool named after the popular BERT language model, that provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations by matching a human-specified input to similar contexts in a large annotated dataset. By aggregating the annotations of the matching similar contexts, exBERT helps intuitively explain what each attention-head has learned.

papers.title: What do language models model? Transformers, automata, and the format of thought
papers.research_question: What do large language models actually model? Do they tell us something about human capacities, or are they models of the corpus we’ve trained them on?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that transformers model the corpus rather than human linguistic capacities, due to the linear format of the residual stream, and they do so by emulating shortcut automata as suggested by Liu et al. (2022).
papers.conclusion: Language models are not modeling human thought but have learned to use language as a technology in a different way, by emulating automata that generate the corpus via shortcut solutions.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers exhibit permutation invariance (unmasked) or substring invariance (masked), which implies the residual stream has at most a linear format.
Human cognitive science indicates that linguistic capabilities require supralinear formats for computation.
Therefore, transformers do not process language in the way humans do and do not model human linguistic capacities.
Transformers can be understood as calculating the input-to-state function of an automaton that generates the corpus, using parallel 'shortcut' solutions.
The transformer architecture is powerful because it eschews structured representations in favor of learning transformations that capture the structure of the domain.
papers.limitation:
The paper focuses on very simple LLMs: encoder-only transformers performing next-token autoregressive tasks.
The paper is a draft in progress and the author is not entirely happy with it, though the general argument is stood by.
papers.abstract: What do large language models actually model? Do they tell us something about human capacities, or are they models of the corpus we've trained them on? I give a non-deflationary defence of the latter position. Cognitive science tells us that linguistic capabilities in humans rely supralinear formats for computation. The transformer architecture, by contrast, supports at best a linear formats for processing. This argument will rely primarily on certain invariants of the computational architecture of transformers. I then suggest a positive story about what transformers are doing, focusing on Liu et al. (2022)'s intriguing speculations about shortcut automata. I conclude with why I don't think this is a terribly deflationary story. Language is not (just) a means for expressing inner state but also a kind of 'discourse machine' that lets us make new language given appropriate context. We have learned to use this technology in one way; LLMs have also learned to use it too, but via very different means.

papers.title: Measuring the Mixing of Contextual Information in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How is contextual information mixed across the Transformer architecture, and how can this mixing be measured to provide faithful explanations for model predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ALTI, an interpretability method that measures token-to-token interactions within each Transformer layer and aggregates them to provide input attribution scores, demonstrating more faithful explanations and increased robustness than gradient-based methods.
papers.conclusion: ALTI is a powerful interpretability method that quantifies the mixing of information in the Transformer, providing faithful input attributions and opening new possibilities for studying contextual information aggregation.
papers.key_findings:
ALTI outperforms gradient-based and other attribution methods in faithfulness metrics (comprehensiveness and sufficiency) across multiple models and datasets.
ALTI provides more robust interpretations across models with identical architecture but different random initializations, as measured by Jaccard similarity and Spearman correlation.
Using ℓ1 norm for measuring token contributions in ALTI is beneficial due to the anisotropic nature of Transformer representations and the presence of outlier dimensions.
The proposed layer-wise contribution measurement (based on distance to the output) significantly improves upon a previous norm-based approach.
Including the second layer normalization (from the feed-forward module) in the analysis has negligible impact on the faithfulness of the interpretations.
papers.limitation:
ALTI does not consider the classifier on top of the Transformer and therefore does not provide explanations for each of the output classes, unlike gradient-based methods.
Faithfulness is evaluated only via sufficiency and comprehensiveness metrics.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture aggregates input information through the self-attention mechanism, but there is no clear understanding of how this information is mixed across the entire model. Additionally, recent works have demonstrated that attention weights alone are not enough to describe the flow of information. In this paper, we consider the whole attention block --multi-head attention, residual connection, and layer normalization-- and define a metric to measure token-to-token interactions within each layer. Then, we aggregate layer-wise interpretations to provide input attribution scores for model predictions. Experimentally, we show that our method, ALTI (Aggregation of Layer-wise Token-to-token Interactions), provides more faithful explanations and increased robustness than gradient-based methods.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn Visual Concepts in Histopathology
papers.research_question: Can self-supervised learning, particularly DINO-based knowledge distillation, learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images?
papers.core_contribution: Vision Transformers using DINO-based self-supervised learning learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images, with different attention heads capturing distinct morphological phenotypes.
papers.conclusion: Self-supervised learning, particularly DINO, is effective for learning representations in histopathology, and the attention heads of Vision Transformers provide interpretable visual concepts that can aid in biomarker discovery.
papers.key_findings:
ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 features are a strong baseline, achieving comparable performance to self-supervised methods on many tasks.
Self-supervised features, particularly from DINO, are robust and sample-efficient, performing well with less training data.
DINO outperforms SimCLR on weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks in histopathology.
DINO's attention heads learn distinct morphological visual concepts, localizing cells, stroma tissue, and fat/air pockets.
papers.limitation: Performance benefit of self-supervised learning may vary depending on organ type (only breast tissue tested) and weakly-supervised architecture (only CLAM tested).
future_direction: Assess the utility of self-supervised methods for learning representations of histopathological images from rare diseases with data paucity of slide-level and patch-level annotations.
papers.abstract: Tissue phenotyping is a fundamental task in learning objective characterizations of histopathologic biomarkers within the tumor-immune microenvironment in cancer pathology. However, whole-slide imaging (WSI) is a complex computer vision in which: 1) WSIs have enormous image resolutions with precludes large-scale pixel-level efforts in data curation, and 2) diversity of morphological phenotypes results in inter- and intra-observer variability in tissue labeling. To address these limitations, current efforts have proposed using pretrained image encoders (transfer learning from ImageNet, self-supervised pretraining) in extracting morphological features from pathology, but have not been extensively validated. In this work, we conduct a search for good representations in pathology by training a variety of self-supervised models with validation on a variety of weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks. Our key finding is in discovering that Vision Transformers using DINO-based knowledge distillation are able to learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images wherein the different attention heads learn distinct morphological phenotypes. We make evaluation code and pretrained weights publicly-available at: https://github.com/Richarizardd/Self-Supervised-ViT-Path.

papers.title: From Tokens to Thoughts: How LLMs and Humans Trade Compression for Meaning
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how LLMs and humans balance compression and meaning in conceptual representation, specifically examining the alignment of LLM-emergent categories with human-defined categories, the fidelity to fine-grained semantic structure like typicality, and the differences in compression-meaning trade-off strategies.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs and humans employ different strategies in the compression-meaning trade-off: LLMs achieve broad categorical alignment but optimize for aggressive statistical compression at the cost of semantic nuance, while humans maintain 'inefficient' representations that preserve rich contextual structure. Encoder models surprisingly outperform much larger decoder models in human alignment.
papers.conclusion: LLMs and humans optimize differently for compression versus meaning preservation, with LLMs favoring statistical efficiency and humans favoring adaptive utility. This divergence highlights the need for AI models that preserve conceptual 'inefficiencies' essential for human-like understanding.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs capture broad categorical boundaries aligned with human categories but show weak correlation with fine-grained typicality judgments.
LLMs achieve more optimal information-theoretic compression (lower L objective) than human conceptual structures.
Encoder models (e.g., BERT) match or exceed the human-alignment performance of decoder models 100x larger, indicating distinct representational mechanisms for understanding vs. generation.
Training dynamics analysis of OLMo-7B reveals a two-phase trajectory: rapid initial concept formation followed by architectural reorganization where semantic processing migrates to mid-network layers.
Human categories appear less statistically efficient but are optimized for adaptive flexibility and rich semantic preservation, unlike LLMs which prioritize compression.
papers.limitation:
The metrics used capture information-compression trade-off and geometric efficiency but do not directly measure all aspects of human-style conceptual abstraction or reasoning.
The analysis is limited to open-source models, excluding closed-source frontier models such as GPT-5 and Claude.
future_direction: Incorporate hierarchical and compositional structure to capture nested relationships between categories.
Incorporate feature- and relation-based biases to help models focus on meaningful perceptual or functional attributes.
Incorporate theory- or causally grounded priors to constrain learning and support flexible generalization.
papers.abstract: Humans organize knowledge into compact conceptual categories that balance compression with semantic richness. Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit impressive linguistic abilities, but whether they navigate this same compression-meaning trade-off remains unclear. We apply an Information Bottleneck framework to compare human conceptual structure with embeddings from 40+ LLMs using classic categorization benchmarks. We find that LLMs broadly align with human category boundaries, yet fall short on fine-grained semantic distinctions. Unlike humans, who maintain ``inefficient'' representations that preserve contextual nuance, LLMs aggressively compress, achieving more optimal information-theoretic compression at the cost of semantic richness. Surprisingly, encoder models outperform much larger decoder models in human alignment, suggesting that understanding and generation rely on distinct representational mechanisms. Training-dynamics analysis reveals a two-phase trajectory: rapid initial concept formation followed by architectural reorganization, during which semantic processing migrates from deep to mid-network layers as the model discovers increasingly efficient, sparser encodings. These divergent strategies, where LLMs optimize for compression and humans for adaptive utility, reveal fundamental differences between artificial and natural intelligence. This highlights the need for models that preserve the conceptual ``inefficiencies'' essential for human-like understanding.

papers.title: Disentangling Direction and Magnitude in Transformer Representations: A Double Dissociation Through L2-Matched Perturbation Analysis
papers.research_question: What are the distinct functional roles of direction (orientation) and magnitude (norm) in transformer hidden state representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces L2-matched perturbation analysis to discover a double dissociation: angular perturbations disproportionately damage language modeling loss, while magnitude perturbations disproportionately damage syntactic accuracy, with distinct mechanistic pathways through attention and LayerNorm.
papers.conclusion: Direction and magnitude serve partially distinct computational roles in LayerNorm-based transformers: direction preferentially governs attentional routing, while magnitude encodes structural position and modulates processing intensity through LayerNorm.
papers.key_findings:
Angular perturbations cause up to 42.9× more damage to language modeling loss than magnitude perturbations at equal Euclidean displacement.
Magnitude perturbations cause up to 20.4% greater drop in syntactic accuracy (subject-verb agreement) than angular perturbations.
Causal intervention shows angular damage is substantially mediated by attention pathways (28.4% recovery via repair), while magnitude damage is substantially mediated by LayerNorm pathways (29.9% recovery).
The dissociation pattern replicates across scales within the Pythia architecture family but reverses in RMSNorm-based architectures like TinyLlama.
Magnitude correlates with parse tree depth, and disrupting this correlation explains why magnitude perturbations specifically impair syntactic processing.
papers.limitation:
L2 matching assumes equal Euclidean distance makes perturbations comparable, but neural networks operate in anisotropic spaces; angular perturbations amplify 3× more than magnitude by the final layer.
Angular perturbations use random orthogonal directions; results might differ for systematic rotations toward known feature directions.
Findings are specific to the Pythia/OPT architecture family and do not generalize to all transformers; the pattern reverses in RMSNorm-based architectures (TinyLlama).
Only middle layers (8–15) were targeted for intervention; early and late layers may show different patterns.
Syntactic evaluation is limited to subject-verb agreement from BLiMP; other syntactic phenomena may show different patterns.
Causal repair experiments account for only ~30% of each perturbation's damage; the remaining ~70% likely flows through MLP layers and residual connections.
future_direction: Feature-specific rotations (systematic rotations toward/away from known feature directions).
Investigating how the roles of direction and magnitude evolve during training.
Exploring magnitude as a confidence signal for uncertainty quantification.
Extending the methodology to other modalities (e.g., vision transformers).
Systematic comparison across normalization schemes (LayerNorm vs. RMSNorm).
papers.abstract: Transformer hidden states encode information as high-dimensional vectors, yet whether direction (orientation in representational space) and magnitude (vector norm) serve distinct functional roles remains unclear. Studying Pythia-family models, we discover a striking cross-over dissociation: angular perturbations cause up to 42.9 more damage to language modeling loss, while magnitude perturbations cause disproportionately more damage to syntactic processing (20.4% vs.1.6% accuracy drop on subject-verb agreement).This finding is enabled by L2-matched perturbation analysis, a methodology ensuring that an gular and magnitude perturbations achieve identical Euclidean displacements. Causal intervention reveals that angular damage flows substantially through the attention pathways (28.4% loss recovery via attention repair), while magnitude damage flows partly through the LayerNorm pathways(29.9% recovery via LayerNorm repair). These patterns replicate across scales within the Pythia architecture family. These findings provide evidence that direction and magnitude support partially distinct computational roles in LayerNorm based architectures. The direction preferentially affects attentional routing, while magnitude modulates processing intensity for fine-grained syntactic judgments. We find different patterns in RMSNorm-based architectures, suggesting that the dissociation depends on architectural choices. Our results refine the linear representation hypothesis and have implications for model editing and interpretability research

papers.title: How Syntax Specialization Emerges in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does syntactic specialization emerge and evolve over training, and how do model initialization, scale, and training data shape this development?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Syntactic Sensitivity Index (SSI) to measure syntactic specialization in language models, revealing that syntactic sensitivity emerges gradually, concentrates in specific layers, exhibits a critical period, and is consistent across architectures but implemented by different neurons.
papers.conclusion: Provides the first systematic, mechanistic account of how syntactic specialization emerges in transformer language models by introducing SSI and applying it across training trajectories, seeds, and model scales, offering an integrated picture of when, where, and how syntax is represented.
papers.key_findings:
SSI correlates with grammaticality judgment accuracy and outperforms supervised probing methods like SVM and regression.
Syntactic specialization emerges gradually during training, with different syntactic phenomena showing distinct acquisition timelines and layer profiles.
There is a critical period (around 16 million tokens) during which syntactic specialization rapidly emerges and then stabilizes.
While layer-level syntactic representations converge across different random seeds, the specific neurons responsible for syntax sensitivity differ (convergent layers, divergent neurons).
Larger models and more training data enhance syntactic abstraction and specialization, but the effect varies across syntactic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Relies on sentence embeddings (mean pooling) which may miss token-level nuance or positional dynamics.
BLiMP focuses on binary acceptability, leaving gradient judgments, semantic-pragmatic interactions, and multi-sentence structures underexplored.
Open theoretical questions about minimal inductive bias, architectural interventions, and relation to semantic grounding.
future_direction: Extend SSI to token-level activations or attention maps.
Explore gradient judgments, semantic-pragmatic interactions, and multi-sentence structures beyond binary acceptability.
Investigate the minimal inductive bias or data regime required for syntactic specialization, architectural interventions, and how syntactic development relates to semantic grounding.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been found to develop surprising internal specializations: Individual neurons, attention heads, and circuits become selectively sensitive to syntactic structure, reflecting patterns observed in the human brain. While this specialization is well-documented, how it emerges during training and what influences its development remains largely unknown. In this work, we tap into the black box of specialization by tracking its formation over time. By quantifying internal syntactic consistency across minimal pairs from various syntactic phenomena, we identify a clear developmental trajectory: Syntactic sensitivity emerges gradually, concentrates in specific layers, and exhibits a 'critical period' of rapid internal specialization. This process is consistent across architectures and initialization parameters (e.g., random seeds), and is influenced by model scale and training data. We therefore reveal not only where syntax arises in LLMs but also how some models internalize it during training. To support future research, we will release the code, models, and training checkpoints upon acceptance.

papers.title: On Efficient Transformer-Based Image Pre-training for Low-Level Vision
papers.research_question: How does pre-training act in image processing systems (low-level vision tasks) and what are effective pre-training strategies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes how pre-training affects internal representations in low-level vision tasks and finds that multi-related-task pre-training is more effective and data-efficient than other strategies.
papers.conclusion: Pre-training plays a central role in developing stronger intermediate representations by incorporating more local information, and its effect is task-specific. Multi-related-task pre-training is highly effective and data-efficient for low-level vision.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-training introduces more local information to higher layers in super-resolution and deraining, yielding significant performance gains, while it hardly affects internal feature representations in denoising, resulting in limited gains.
Multi-related-task pre-training is more effective and data-efficient than single-task or multi-unrelated-task pre-training.
Larger model capacities generally obtain more improvements from pre-training.
Transformers benefit more from pre-training than CNNs, providing higher performance baselines with fewer parameters.
The internal representations of SR and deraining models show clear stages (more local in early layers, more global in higher layers), while denoising models present a relatively uniform structure filled with local information.
papers.limitation:
The study mainly investigates pre-training on synthesized data; future research should explore real-world settings and more tasks, extended to video processing.
The encoder-decoder design uses a fixed downsampling strategy, which may not be optimal for all degradation levels; adaptive downsampling could be better.
future_direction: Explore pre-training in real-world settings and more tasks.
Extend the study to video processing.
Investigate adaptive downsampling based on degradation degrees.
papers.abstract: Pre-training has marked numerous state of the arts in high-level computer vision, while few attempts have ever been made to investigate how pre-training acts in image processing systems. In this paper, we tailor transformer-based pre-training regimes that boost various low-level tasks. To comprehensively diagnose the influence of pre-training, we design a whole set of principled evaluation tools that uncover its effects on internal representations. The observations demonstrate that pre-training plays strikingly different roles in low-level tasks. For example, pre-training introduces more local information to higher layers in super-resolution (SR), yielding significant performance gains, while pre-training hardly affects internal feature representations in denoising, resulting in limited gains. Further, we explore different methods of pre-training, revealing that multi-related-task pre-training is more effective and data-efficient than other alternatives. Finally, we extend our study to varying data scales and model sizes, as well as comparisons between transformers and CNNs-based architectures. Based on the study, we successfully develop state-of-the-art models for multiple low-level tasks. Code is released at https://github.com/fenglinglwb/EDT.

papers.title: How Large Language Models Encode Context Knowledge? A Layer-Wise Probing Study
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode context knowledge across different layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a layer-wise probing framework to study how LLMs encode context knowledge, finding that more context knowledge is encoded in upper layers and that knowledge-related entity tokens encode knowledge earlier, with knowledge spreading to other tokens via attention.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a novel layer-wise probing framework for explaining how LLMs encode context knowledge, demonstrating that LLMs encode more knowledge in upper layers and transfer knowledge from entity tokens to other tokens, with retention diminishing with irrelevant evidence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers.
LLMs primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers.
LLMs gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence.
Base models have lower capability to encode knowledge through prompting compared to chat models.
The long-term memory capability of LLMs degrades when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical mechanism behind the observed phenomena remains an open issue.
Experiments are limited to LLaMA 2 models, ignoring other SOTA models.
future_direction: Mathematical understanding of the role of self-attention in knowledge transfer.
Experiments on more PLMs (e.g., PaLM, OPT, Pythia).
papers.abstract: Previous work has showcased the intriguing capability of large language models (LLMs) in retrieving facts and processing context knowledge. However, only limited research exists on the layer-wise capability of LLMs to encode knowledge, which challenges our understanding of their internal mechanisms. In this paper, we devote the first attempt to investigate the layer-wise capability of LLMs through probing tasks. We leverage the powerful generative capability of ChatGPT to construct probing datasets, providing diverse and coherent evidence corresponding to various facts. We employ $\mathcal V$-usable information as the validation metric to better reflect the capability in encoding context knowledge across different layers. Our experiments on conflicting and newly acquired knowledge show that LLMs: (1) prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers; (2) primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers; and (3) gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Jometeorie/probing_llama.

papers.title: Revisiting Entropy Rate Constancy in Text
